channel.title: The Brief — Adam's News
channel.description: Every story from Adam's three daily briefs (9 AM / 5 PM / 10 PM CT) as its own item, readable right in your feed reader, with a link to the original article.

item.title: Russia pounds Ukraine's grid as Abu Dhabi talks open — and end day one still split
item.description:
Russia hit Ukraine's power grid again overnight, killing two people and knocking out substations across the country, on the very morning Russian, Ukrainian and American negotiators sat down in Abu Dhabi for their first three-way talks since February. By the end of day one, the positions were exactly where they started: Moscow wants the shape of a future European security order agreed before any ceasefire, Kyiv wants the shooting to stop first, and the land question hasn't moved at all.
Russian forces struck 10 Ukrainian regions overnight, hitting five major electrical substations that move power between regions — in Poltava, Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia and Kirovohrad — according to Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi. Two people were killed in the Vinnytsia region. State grid operator Ukrenergo said energy infrastructure was hit in eight regions overnight and into the morning, leaving homes without power in six, including Kyiv, Kharkiv and Dnipropetrovsk. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 162 drones and a ballistic missile overnight. The Guardian's live blog, citing the Kyiv Independent, reported at least nine people killed and 39 injured across Ukraine over the past day. Russia's defence ministry said its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight over eight Russian regions and Crimea, and said it struck cargo vessels and a tanker in the Black Sea, including a ship east of Odesa.
The talks themselves opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday with the US envoy Jared Kushner telling reporters that almost daily contacts with both sides had "narrowed the gaps" and that the Americans had "some good ideas on how to bridge it" — but he stopped short of promising a settlement. The Russian delegation is led by Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, Ukraine's by foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, with presidential office chief Kyrylo Budanov also taking part. Ukrainian negotiators spent roughly two months preparing, Umerov said, and Kyiv's mandate covers "all the issues", with security guarantees the priority.
What each side argues is now on the record, and the two positions pull in opposite directions. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said after the day's session that Russia would not agree to an immediate ceasefire without knowing what would happen next — in Moscow's telling, the outlines of a future European security architecture should be agreed first, and only then should the fighting stop. Kyiv and its European backers want the reverse: Ukraine is seeking binding assurances that Russia will not invade again and wants the fighting to stop, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday that any meaningful discussion of Europe's security architecture can only come once a ceasefire is achieved. On territory, Moscow wants Ukraine to withdraw from the parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson that it claims to have annexed; Kyiv refuses to cede territory and has proposed freezing the conflict along the current front line. US officials have said both sides showed "a little bit of flexibility" in private, but neither government has said anything similar in public, and President Trump has publicly suggested Ukraine will end up with "a little bit different shape" — a remark Kyiv has not welcomed.
Europe's place at the table was contested all week. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov insisted the format is strictly three-way, and Kushner described the Europeans as being kept informed on the sidelines, with a wider format only after progress is made. Even so, European officials from the UK, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission met the US and Ukrainian teams in Abu Dhabi, and a joint statement said any settlement must respect Ukraine's sovereignty, territorial integrity and independent decision-making, and that a strong NATO will continue to be central to collective Euro-Atlantic security. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Europe does not need to establish a new security architecture.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the overnight strikes are the point, not the talks. The grid attacks are part of a renewed air campaign as winter approaches, and Moscow has expanded its targeting in recent months to businesses, consumer logistics and other economic targets — a home improvement store in Kirovohrad was hit overnight — in a bid to weaken the war effort. Homes across six regions woke up without power, and Ukraine has struggled to intercept the fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. One small humanitarian step stands out against that: a six-day local ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky at the end of October and beginning of November allowed civilians to leave and aid to get in, and the US says it will keep working on prisoner exchanges and other humanitarian issues.
In short: the first three-way talks in nine months opened in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and ended day one with the same split — Moscow wants a security order agreed before a ceasefire, Kyiv wants the ceasefire first, and neither side has budged on territory — while Russia kept hitting Ukraine's power grid overnight, killing two people and cutting power in six regions. The second session is Wednesday, and Washington has signalled it may follow Abu Dhabi with separate meetings with Putin and Zelensky.
Sources:
Source: tbsnews.net.

item.title: Houthis/Saudi — overnight update: drone downed over Eastern Province, Saudi jets hit Sanaa
item.description:
The overnight exchange covered in the night brief — three Houthi missiles intercepted, two aimed at Riyadh and one at the south — had two additions on Tuesday morning.
The coalition later said it also intercepted and destroyed a drone over Saudi Arabia's oil-rich Eastern Province, and the Houthi-run Saba news agency reported Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa, hitting the al-Mufazir gas station in the Jadar district north of the capital and a building belonging to the state oil company in southern Sanaa. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the Sanaa strikes, and the Houthis did not immediately claim the overnight launches.
No casualties were reported from the interceptions. (Reuters via RadioCMS)
Source: 1502-6478b717a4a2f.radiocms.com.

item.title: Iran — Canada reimposes sanctions; US answer still due today
item.description:
Canada reimposed sanctions on 11 Iranian entities on Tuesday for contributing to Iran's nuclear activities and ballistic missile programme, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said.
The list includes Iran's Nuclear Fuel Production and Procurement Company, the Nuclear Reactors Fuel Company, the National Iranian Oil Company and the National Iranian Tanker Company. The US answer to Tehran's two-day Hormuz proposal is still expected today, with Qatari officials due in Tehran the same day.
Iran has not responded to the single-source report of a phased US offer (partial blockade lift first, then nuclear talks), and Tehran's own officials remain split — Pezeshkian talking negotiation, security chief Rezaei calling talk of a deal "fake news". (Reuters)
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Israel — new Knesset sworn in today; opposition picks Kahana for speaker
item.description:
Israel's 26th Knesset is sworn in this afternoon, with 46 of its 120 members serving for the first time.
Hours before the ceremony, the opposition bloc chose Matan Kahana of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party as its candidate for Knesset speaker, in a bid to take control of parliament from Amir Ohana of Netanyahu's Likud. At least 61 lawmakers must sign a request or vote to replace the speaker.
Eisenkot, who received the mandate to form a government on Sunday, has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. Netanyahu remains prime minister of a caretaker government until a new coalition is sworn in.
(The Insight International · 10News)
Source: theinsightinternational.com.

item.title: Khor Mor — still shut, no restart date; US envoy condemns the attack
item.description:
Production at the Khor Mor gas field in Iraqi Kurdistan remained suspended on Tuesday, with operator Dana Gas still assessing damage from Sunday night's drone strike and giving no restart date.
The strike cut 2,500–2,800 MW — roughly 70–80% of the region's power — and Baghdad has ordered household gas supplies to the region until the field restarts. A US presidential envoy condemned the attack on Tuesday.
No group has claimed responsibility. (Silent Dossier · JBizNews)
Source: silentdossier.com.

item.title: Nvidia unveils GR00T 2, a robot model that learns by watching humans
item.description:
Nvidia introduced GR00T 2 at the Conference on Robot Learning in Austin on Monday, November 9 — an open world-action model for robots, built on its Cosmos platform, that learns new manipulation skills largely from watching videos of humans do the job.
The model was trained on robot data plus 100,000 hours of open-source egocentric human video, which Nvidia released as the Human-1M-100K dataset under a Creative Commons licence. Nvidia reports the model completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once with no task-specific demonstrations, averaged 71% success with one demonstration per task and 95% with five — its own figures, for 50 tasks it has not named.
The model code is due in December and no weights release date or licence has been announced, so "open" is for now more of a promise than a download. Alongside it, Isaac Lab 3.0 adds a Newton physics option and reinforcement post-training, with up to 2.5× training throughput on a dexterous-manipulation benchmark.
(NVIDIA Developer Forums · TechTimes · Poyo AI Daily)
Source: forums.developer.nvidia.com.

item.title: Anthropic retracted its IPO pricing hours before the roadshow
item.description:
Anthropic sent banks a securities filing late Monday showing about 866.7 million Class A shares at $70 to $80 each — implying up to $69.3 billion in proceeds at the top of the range, plus a separate $26 billion private placement from Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC — then emailed back saying the pricing details were "inaccurate" and that it would update the filing later.
Reuters, which saw the emails, could not determine what was wrong, and Anthropic declined to comment. The roadshow is still expected to start today, Tuesday, with pricing the following week.
The $69.3 billion figure is a draft number the company disowned, not a confirmed IPO size. (Reuters via The Hindu BusinessLine · Unite.AI)
Source: thehindubusinessline.com.

item.title: Nvidia — Monday's sell-off wiped about $250 billion off its value
item.description:
Nvidia shares fell on Monday after CEO Jensen Huang's admission of an affair with a woman US officials allege was a Chinese intelligence asset, wiping roughly $250 billion from the company's market value, according to AI-news roundups this morning.
The board's independent investigation continues, House chairs want an answer by Wednesday, November 11, on a closed-door briefing November 18, and Nvidia reports Q3 earnings November 17. Catch-up: the Financial Times reported on November 3 that Nvidia has verbally told its global cloud partners to sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers — a cap on the overseas-rental route Chinese firms use to reach advanced chips — applying to new contracts only, with Nvidia neither confirming nor denying the 51% figure.
(Kill The AI · Clash Report)
Source: killtheai.com.

item.title: Xen Orchestra critical auth bypass is being actively exploited — patch now
item.description:
Vates published a critical advisory on Tuesday for Xen Orchestra (VSA-2026-062): an empty-object login token in REST cookie handling lets an attacker bypass authentication entirely and act with admin privilege, and from there take over managed XCP-ng pools and nodes as root.
Vates says the flaw is actively exploited by a threat actor operating from 91.211.251.112:8001 and a Tor onion address, and that exploitation by other actors can't be ruled out. Affected: xo-server before 5.213.1, and 5.213.2 in Xen Orchestra before 6.9.1 (stable) and 6.10.0 (latest).
Fixed in Xen Orchestra 6.9.1 and 6.10.0, released today. (Vates advisory · Your Cyber Brief)
Source: docs.vates.tech.

item.title: Barracuda confirms exploitation hitting a small number of organisations
item.description:
Barracuda's advisory, updated November 9, says it has identified exploitation affecting a small number of organisations on specified appliances with vulnerable firmware and an attacker-accessible admin interface.
Patches are out for the named appliances; Barracuda has not named the victims or described the evidence in detail. (Your Cyber Brief)
Source: yourcyberbrief.com.

item.title: Plex2Shell — catch-up: QNAP warned last week that unpatched Plex servers are being hit
item.description:
QNAP warned on November 6 that attackers are actively exploiting the Plex2Shell chain — four chained flaws (CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, CVE-2026-96656) in Plex Media Server — against internet-exposed NAS devices, gaining unauthenticated remote code execution via port 32400. CISA added all four to its KEV catalog on October 20. Over 36,000 internet-exposed Plex servers were identified as unpatched, and QNAP says patching alone won't remove backdoors already installed — affected users should treat devices and stored data as fully compromised and do a clean reinstall. Fix: Plex 1.43.3.10861 or later. (All About Cookies · Aviatrix)
No new CISA KEV additions since the four added Monday (GPUStack, FreeSWITCH, OpenSSH "SSHole", IBM Aspera Faspex) — federal remediation deadline for those four is Thursday, November 12.
Source: allaboutcookies.org.

item.title: Farwell jury goes back to deliberate today — judge expected to give an Allen charge
item.description:
The federal jury in former Stoughton detective Matthew Farwell's murder trial — accused of killing Sandra Birchmore, 23 and pregnant, in 2021 and staging it as a suicide — resumes deliberating today after telling the judge on Monday it was deadlocked after about 10½ hours and did not expect that to change. Judge Denise Casper sent the panel home Monday afternoon; former Massachusetts AG Martha Coakley said the judge will most likely give an "Allen charge" today, instructing holdout jurors to listen to the other side. A conviction on either count carries a mandatory life sentence. (Particle · Vinnie Politan)
No fresh developments: FTC v. Amazon Prime jury trial continues in Seattle; Netanyahu trial (Mandelblit testimony resumes October 18–22 — no session today); Murdaugh retrial (next hearing November 13). Krakow: no fresh developments; post-mortems on the nine victims began Monday and were expected to take about two days.
Source: particle.news.

item.title: Open source — GitHub trending, November 10
item.description:
Sherlock still leads the daily chart (~107k stars, +4.3k in 24h), followed by Meta's Astryx design system (~20k, +3.3k) and OpenMausBot (~19.7k, +1.6k).
New on the lists: huamidev/GestaltX, a MobileGestalt editor for iOS 27.x that flips hidden iPhone switches (region code, Dynamic Island, always-on display) with an automatic backup before every write; Minireel/HGhub, a third-party YellowFruit client; janestreet/agent_skills (+424 today); and garrytan/gbrain. MuJoCo 4.0 (Google DeepMind's physics engine) sits at ~16.9k.
(GitDiscover · Daily Diff · GhTrends)
Source: gitdiscover.org.

item.title: Houthis hit Riyadh again on Monday night — missiles intercepted, oil pipeline struck
item.description:
The Houthis fired more missiles at Saudi Arabia on Monday night, hours after the kingdom said its key East-West oil pipeline had been struck — the latest round in a campaign that has now hit Riyadh's financial district, its main airport, Aramco's headquarters and now a pipeline in the space of a few weeks.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Tuesday morning that its air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile and a cruise missile fired at Riyadh, and a second ballistic missile aimed at the country's southern region. Saudi Civil Defence had issued early-warning alerts for the capital and for the southwestern cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait before the interceptions, then said the danger had passed. Multiple explosions were heard in Riyadh, according to AFP, and residents received text-message alerts telling them to take shelter. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on Monday night's launches, and no casualties were reported.
The pipeline strike came earlier on Monday. Saudi Arabia said its East-West oil pipeline was struck in the Medina region, causing a limited fire that was later extinguished. The attack caused no casualties and did not affect pipeline operations, the state news agency SPA said. The East-West line is one of the kingdom's most important pieces of energy infrastructure — it moves crude from the Gulf coast to the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz — so even a limited strike on it is a deliberate escalation in targeting. It followed Sunday's attack on Riyadh, when falling debris from an attempted missile strike blew out windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower in the King Abdullah Financial District. Early on Tuesday, Riyadh's deputy governor, Prince Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Abdulaziz, inspected the damaged Aramco building and said the attack showed the Houthis were targeting civilian facilities.
The two sides' accounts of the damage keep diverging. Saudi officials have described the Aramco Tower damage as limited and caused by falling debris, while BBC Verify's footage showed windows blown out across several floors — more than "minor damage" — and the Houthis have claimed direct hits on the tower, the airport, Aramco storage facilities and the eastern city of Abqaiq. The Houthis say they are hitting Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities in support of Iran's war with the US and Israel; Riyadh says it is responding with airstrikes on Houthi targets in Yemen, including launchers in Saada and Sanaa. Neither side's claims about what was hit and what was intercepted can be fully verified from the ground, and the coalition has not said whether Monday night's missiles were aimed at the airport, the financial district or elsewhere in the capital.
For ordinary people in Riyadh, the pattern is now familiar and wearing: sirens and shelter texts, explosions overhead, then an all-clear — twice in two days, and the fourth attack on the capital's infrastructure in about a week. King Khalid International Airport has been closed or disrupted for most of the past month, and the pipeline strike is a reminder that the campaign is widening beyond airports and office towers toward the energy system itself. The Houthis have stepped up their strikes since advancing toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, and there is no sign either side is easing off — the coalition keeps destroying launchers, and the Houthis keep launching.
In short: the Houthis fired three more missiles at Saudi Arabia on Monday night — two at Riyadh, one at the south — all intercepted according to the coalition, and the East-West oil pipeline was struck earlier in the day with a limited fire and no disruption to operations. No casualties were reported, the Houthis have not commented on the latest launches, and the pattern of near-daily attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure continues.
Sources:
Source: ksevradio.com.
item.content:encoded:
The Houthis fired more missiles at Saudi Arabia on Monday night, hours after the kingdom said its key East-West oil pipeline had been struck — the latest round in a campaign that has now hit Riyadh's financial district, its main airport, Aramco's headquarters and now a pipeline in the space of a few weeks.

The Saudi-led coalition said on Tuesday morning that its air defences intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile and a cruise missile fired at Riyadh, and a second ballistic missile aimed at the country's southern region. Saudi Civil Defence had issued early-warning alerts for the capital and for the southwestern cities of Abha and Khamis Mushait before the interceptions, then said the danger had passed. Multiple explosions were heard in Riyadh, according to AFP, and residents received text-message alerts telling them to take shelter. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on Monday night's launches, and no casualties were reported.

The pipeline strike came earlier on Monday. Saudi Arabia said its East-West oil pipeline was struck in the Medina region, causing a limited fire that was later extinguished. The attack caused no casualties and did not affect pipeline operations, the state news agency SPA said. The East-West line is one of the kingdom's most important pieces of energy infrastructure — it moves crude from the Gulf coast to the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz — so even a limited strike on it is a deliberate escalation in targeting. It followed Sunday's attack on Riyadh, when falling debris from an attempted missile strike blew out windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower in the King Abdullah Financial District. Early on Tuesday, Riyadh's deputy governor, Prince Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Abdulaziz, inspected the damaged Aramco building and said the attack showed the Houthis were targeting civilian facilities.

The two sides' accounts of the damage keep diverging. Saudi officials have described the Aramco Tower damage as limited and caused by falling debris, while BBC Verify's footage showed windows blown out across several floors — more than "minor damage" — and the Houthis have claimed direct hits on the tower, the airport, Aramco storage facilities and the eastern city of Abqaiq. The Houthis say they are hitting Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities in support of Iran's war with the US and Israel; Riyadh says it is responding with airstrikes on Houthi targets in Yemen, including launchers in Saada and Sanaa. Neither side's claims about what was hit and what was intercepted can be fully verified from the ground, and the coalition has not said whether Monday night's missiles were aimed at the airport, the financial district or elsewhere in the capital.

For ordinary people in Riyadh, the pattern is now familiar and wearing: sirens and shelter texts, explosions overhead, then an all-clear — twice in two days, and the fourth attack on the capital's infrastructure in about a week. King Khalid International Airport has been closed or disrupted for most of the past month, and the pipeline strike is a reminder that the campaign is widening beyond airports and office towers toward the energy system itself. The Houthis have stepped up their strikes since advancing toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, and there is no sign either side is easing off — the coalition keeps destroying launchers, and the Houthis keep launching.

In short: the Houthis fired three more missiles at Saudi Arabia on Monday night — two at Riyadh, one at the south — all intercepted according to the coalition, and the East-West oil pipeline was struck earlier in the day with a limited fire and no disruption to operations. No casualties were reported, the Houthis have not commented on the latest launches, and the pattern of near-daily attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure continues.

item.title: Iran — US reportedly offered a phased deal; Tehran's own officials split on talks
item.description:
Two new wrinkles in the Iran standoff on Monday. The Emirati outlet Erem News, citing diplomatic sources familiar with the mediated talks, reported that the United States has proposed a phased plan: a partial lifting of its naval blockade of Iran first, then nuclear talks, with a gradual lifting of sanctions and the release of frozen Iranian funds to follow. Iran has not responded to the offer, according to the report, and wants written commitments and tangible steps from Washington first. Neither Washington nor Tehran has confirmed the report — treat it as unconfirmed for now. It is, however, the first sign of a concrete American sequencing offer after weeks of deadlock over whether nuclear talks or sanctions relief comes first.
Tehran, meanwhile, is speaking with two voices. President Pezeshkian said Monday that Supreme Leader Khamenei had ordered officials to end the state of "neither war nor peace" and that Iran would negotiate with dignity. But the Supreme National Security Council's secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, wrote on X the same day rejecting reports of talks as "fake news" and telling Washington to "surrender to the seven conditions Iran has repeatedly set out." Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei defended the two-day proposal at his weekly press conference, asking whether it was unreasonable for Iran to demand sanctions and the blockade be lifted before negotiations start. President Trump, after meeting Qatar's prime minister at the White House, said there was progress toward a deal and described the war as militarily near its end — but in a separate Reuters phone interview he kept the strike option open and said he was content with the naval blockade. A US answer to Tehran is still expected by Tuesday, with Qatari officials due in Tehran the same day.
Sources:
Source: mohintechbd.blogspot.com.

item.title: Ukraine — ISW: Russia claims a village, neither side advanced, and Kyiv's bridges are the target
item.description:
The Institute for the Study of War's November 9 assessment adds a few details to Monday's picture without changing it. Russia's defence ministry claimed the seizure of Vasylkove, northwest of Hulyaipole — its first claim of taking a settlement since October 28 — but ISW records no confirmed advance by either side on November 9. The assessment also notes Russia is leaning into highly manoeuvrable quasi-cruise missiles and modifying anti-aircraft and ballistic missiles to expand ballistic-trajectory strikes, with a Russian military outlet claiming converted RM-48U missiles launched from S-300/S-400 systems were used against Kyiv's Northern and Southern Bridges on November 7 and October 27. The overnight picture stands as reported earlier: 317 drones including 105 jet-powered ones, more than 30 ballistic missiles, four substations hit, and over 600,000 without power in Dnipropetrovsk. No new overnight tally for November 9–10 had been reported by reliable outlets by 10 PM CT. US-brokered talks open in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday.
Sources:
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Israel — Eisenkot and Lieberman find common ground; Knesset sworn in Tuesday
item.description:
Gadi Eisenkot's meeting with Avigdor Lieberman on Monday produced the first concrete agreements of the coalition talks: both men described the talks as positive, they agreed the next Knesset Speaker will come from Eisenkot's Yashar party, and Lieberman will get the first opportunity to negotiate with the ultra-Orthodox parties. Lieberman has ruled out supporting a government that depends on Arab parties, and Eisenkot's bloc holds 48 of 120 seats against the 61 needed. The new Knesset is sworn in on Tuesday, with 54 new members, and there are concerns the proceedings could be disrupted as Netanyahu continues to promote claims that the election was stolen — claims that, outside of Channel 14, do not appear to be gaining traction. Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
Sources:
Source: marcschulman.substack.com.

item.title: Krakow — no fresh developments Monday evening
item.description:
No new developments in the Krakow investigation on Monday evening. Post-mortems on all nine victims began Monday and were expected to take about two days. One of the two wounded police officers remains in a coma while the other has regained consciousness, according to a Monday update. Prosecutors still have not established a motive or an ideology link for gunman Michał O., who died in hospital early Monday and was never questioned.

item.title: Khor Mor — still shut, no restart date
item.description:
Production at the Khor Mor gas field in Iraqi Kurdistan remained suspended on Monday while operator Dana Gas assesses damage from Sunday night's drone strike, which cut 2,500–2,800 MW — roughly 70–80% of the region's power. Baghdad has ordered household gas supplies to the region until the field restarts, and a joint investigation has been ordered. No group has claimed responsibility, and no restart date has been given.

item.title: Google takes over Crusoe's troubled Wyoming data centre — $17 billion planned
item.description:
Google has taken over an unfinished AI data-centre project in southeastern Wyoming from Crusoe, the Denver-based developer that had failed to land Google as a customer for the site.
Crusoe confirmed the sale on Friday, November 6, a day after Google announced plans to invest $17 billion to build its first data-centre campus in the state. Google did not disclose what it paid for the site — the $17 billion is its planned investment in the campus, not a purchase price — and it has not committed to the original 10-gigawatt scale Crusoe had planned with Blackstone-backed Tallgrass.
Google says it will cover 100% of the project's energy needs and infrastructure costs, sourcing power from Bloom Energy natural-gas fuel cells with carbon capture. Crusoe is still developing another data centre for Google near Amarillo, Texas.
(TechCrunch · Inc. · Telecompaper)
Source: techcrunch.com.

item.title: Nvidia — Huang scandal becomes a White House problem, lawmakers demand details
item.description:
The scandal around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset has moved beyond the company's board investigation and into Washington.
TechCrunch reported Monday evening that it is now a concern for the White House, and lawmakers from both parties are demanding details from Nvidia. The board's independent investigation continues, House chairs want an answer by Wednesday, November 11, on a closed-door briefing November 18, and Nvidia reports Q3 earnings November 17.
Nvidia shares fell 4.89% in premarket trading Monday. (TechCrunch via SaveDelete · TokenPost)
Source: savedelete.com.

item.title: Who Gives A Crap — customer data exposed through a marketing supplier
item.description:
Toilet-paper brand Who Gives A Crap told customers over the weekend that their personal information was accessed without authorisation in a breach at one of its US-based marketing software providers.
The access began on October 30, was detected on October 31 and secured by November 1, but the company was not told until November 6 and began notifying customers on November 7. Affected customers are in Australia, the UK and the US; the data includes names, email and postal addresses, phone numbers and total spending with the brand.
Payment details, order details and passwords were not involved, and customer accounts were not directly accessed. The company has not said how many customers were affected, has not named the supplier, and does not yet know whether the data was copied.
The main risk is phishing and scam messages using real customer details. (The Register · Company notice)
Source: theregister.com.

item.title: "SSHole" exploitation count ticks up
item.description:
GreyNoise now records 17 confirmed exploitation chains for the "SSHole" OpenSSH flaw (CVE-2026-123158), up from 16, including attempts to read password hashes and SSH keys, probe cloud metadata and deploy a Python implant.
Alpine's advisory covers releases 3.16 through 3.24 and edge; the fix is OpenSSH 10.6p2 or a distribution patch. CISA's KEV deadline for the four flaws added Monday is November 12, and no new KEV additions were reported after those four.
(Nerds.xyz · CISA via CTXSec)
Source: nerds.xyz.

item.title: Lindsay Clancy can be retried for murder, judge rules
item.description:
A Massachusetts judge ruled on Monday that Lindsay Clancy, the mother of three who killed her children in Duxbury in January 2023, can be tried again for murder.
Judge William F. Sullivan found that the September 4 mistrial — declared after a holdout juror blocked a unanimous verdict — was justified by manifest necessity, so a retrial does not violate the double-jeopardy clause.
Clancy's lawyers had argued she could not be tried again. A hearing on November 16 will discuss timing; the judge has suggested the second trial could be held in March.
(Reuters via Duke FM · USA Today)
Source: duke.fm.

item.title: Farwell jury deadlocked, sent back to deliberate Tuesday
item.description:
The jury in former Stoughton police detective Matthew Farwell's federal murder trial — accused of killing Sandra Birchmore, 23 and pregnant, in 2021 and staging it as a suicide — told the judge on Monday it was deadlocked and did not expect that to change. Jurors had deliberated about 7½ hours on Monday on top of around three hours on Friday. Judge Denise Casper excused the jury at 4:30 p.m. and said she was inclined to let them keep deliberating on Tuesday without further instructions, given the scope of the evidence. (Enterprise News)
No fresh developments in the Netanyahu trial or the Murdaugh retrial (next hearing November 13). The FTC v. Amazon Prime jury trial continues in Seattle; no fresh developments Monday evening beyond the summary-judgment motions reported earlier.
Source: enterprisenews.com.

item.title: Strikes keep coming on the eve of Abu Dhabi talks — and Trump says a deal is "very close"
item.description:
Russia battered Ukraine's power grid again and Ukraine hit another of Russia's biggest refineries plus a missile-fuel plant, hours before US-brokered talks open in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday — and President Trump told CBS's "60 Minutes" on Sunday that the two sides are "very close" to a deal, while hinting Ukraine would end up with "a little bit different shape."
Russia's defence ministry said it targeted four electrical substations in Ukraine's Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Cherkasy and Vinnytsia regions, part of its campaign to deny civilians heating, light and running water as winter approaches. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 317 drones overnight, including 105 jet-powered ones. In Odesa, Russian forces hit a warehouse holding food supplies for kindergartens and schools, killing three people, local officials said. Zelenskyy said Monday the European Union had agreed to activate a special emergency mechanism that speeds up funding for power-grid repairs.
Ukraine's reply was long-range. Drones started a fire at the KINEF oil refinery near St. Petersburg, one of Russia's largest, more than 1,200 kilometres from the Ukrainian border, Leningrad Governor Alexander Drozdenko said. Ukraine's General Staff also said its forces struck a plant near St. Petersburg that produces solid rocket propellant for Russia's Iskander-M ballistic missiles — a direct hit on the weapons Ukraine says it cannot stop in the air without more US-made Patriot interceptors, which are in short supply. Ukraine said in early October that its long-range strikes had already neutralised more than half of Russia's oil refining capacity.
The two sides arrive at the table telling different stories about what the talks are even about. Trump said in the "60 Minutes" interview, which aired Sunday, that Moscow and Kyiv are "very close" to a deal despite the "tremendous hatred" between Putin and Zelenskyy — though, as AP notes, he has previously made statements about developments in the war that haven't materialised. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Monday that Trump's team has placed "collective security" — covering not just Russia and Ukraine but a wider area — at the top of the agenda. Moscow insists Europe will not take part in the three-way talks: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday the meeting would focus on trilateral negotiations with the US mediating, while French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Sunday that France and other European representatives would be in the UAE. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to travel to Abu Dhabi. The last three-way round, in Geneva in February, delivered no significant progress.
For ordinary people, the human cost is measured in cold and dark: hundreds of thousands without power in Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions alone, emergency and scheduled outages across most of Ukraine, and a refinery fire 1,200 kilometres inside Russia that shows nowhere in either country's energy system is out of reach. The 48 hours before the talks brought a massive Russian strike on Ukraine's power system and Ukrainian strikes on Kirishi and a missile-fuel plant in return — the agenda for Abu Dhabi is being written by the attacks themselves.
In short: both sides hit each other's energy and military infrastructure one more time before Tuesday's Abu Dhabi talks, Trump says a deal is "very close" while hinting Ukraine will have to give up territory, and Moscow is trying to keep Europe out of the room — with the last round in Geneva having produced nothing.
Sources:
Source: military.com.

item.title: Trump meets Qatar's prime minister as oil plunges on peace hopes
item.description:
President Trump met Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, at the White House on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the eight-month Iran war ramp up — and oil fell sharply, with Brent settling at $92.57 a barrel, down 5.85% on the day, as traders bet on a diplomatic exit.
The meeting, held behind closed doors at noon ET, put Qatar — the key mediator carrying messages between Washington and Tehran — at the centre of the day. Vice President J.D. Vance, who has been speaking almost daily with mediators, also met Sheikh Mohammed separately. The Qatari leader visited Tehran last week and has been pushing a compressed two-day framework: the US ends its blockade of Iranian ports, eases some sanctions and halts bombing, and Iran stops its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, with talks on its nuclear programme to follow. Washington has repeatedly rejected that sequencing, insisting nuclear issues come first.
Tehran, for its part, sounded more open on Monday. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran was prepared to negotiate an end to what he called a prolonged state of "neither war nor peace," adding that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had instructed officials to end the uncertainty — while insisting Iran would not surrender to coercion. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman defended the two-day proposal on Monday as the most reasonable offer on the table. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday he could not say the two sides were "on the verge of a breakthrough" and called Tehran's demands "unacceptable," "outrageous" and "ridiculous." A US official told Al Jazeera the indirect discussions were "positive and constructive" but stressed there would be no agreement unless Iran's nuclear programme is addressed.
The two sides' versions of the stall still do not agree on the cause. Araghchi said mediators had made no progress since the "shock" of the US midterm elections; Rubio said there had been little productive result so far. Behind the public statements, Qatari officials are expected to continue discussions in Tehran on Tuesday, and Araghchi said he hoped to receive Washington's final response by Tuesday. Meanwhile, the UAE revealed a major surge in oil exports despite the conflict, and the US blockade of Iranian ports continues to bite — Iraq's foreign minister said it has cost Iraq $60 billion.
For the world economy, the shipping war is the part that bites — and the part markets are now pricing as easing. Iran closed the strait — which handled roughly 20% of the world's oil and gas before the war — shortly after the US and Israel launched their offensive on February 28, and flows are running well below capacity. item.content:encoded:
President Trump met Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, at the White House on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the eight-month Iran war ramp up — and oil fell sharply, with Brent settling at $92.57 a barrel, down 5.85% on the day, as traders bet on a diplomatic exit.

The meeting, held behind closed doors at noon ET, put Qatar — the key mediator carrying messages between Washington and Tehran — at the centre of the day. Vice President J.D. Vance, who has been speaking almost daily with mediators, also met Sheikh Mohammed separately. The Qatari leader visited Tehran last week and has been pushing a compressed two-day framework: the US ends its blockade of Iranian ports, eases some sanctions and halts bombing, and Iran stops its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, with talks on its nuclear programme to follow. Washington has repeatedly rejected that sequencing, insisting nuclear issues come first.

Tehran, for its part, sounded more open on Monday. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran was prepared to negotiate an end to what he called a prolonged state of "neither war nor peace," adding that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had instructed officials to end the uncertainty — while insisting Iran would not surrender to coercion. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman defended the two-day proposal on Monday as the most reasonable offer on the table. But Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday he could not say the two sides were "on the verge of a breakthrough" and called Tehran's demands "unacceptable," "outrageous" and "ridiculous." A US official told Al Jazeera the indirect discussions were "positive and constructive" but stressed there would be no agreement unless Iran's nuclear programme is addressed.

The two sides' versions of the stall still do not agree on the cause. Araghchi said mediators had made no progress since the "shock" of the US midterm elections; Rubio said there had been little productive result so far. Behind the public statements, Qatari officials are expected to continue discussions in Tehran on Tuesday, and Araghchi said he hoped to receive Washington's final response by Tuesday. Meanwhile, the UAE revealed a major surge in oil exports despite the conflict, and the US blockade of Iranian ports continues to bite — Iraq's foreign minister said it has cost Iraq $60 billion.

For the world economy, the shipping war is the part that bites — and the part markets are now pricing as easing. Iran closed the strait — which handled roughly 20% of the world's oil and gas before the war — shortly after the US and Israel launched their offensive on February 28, and flows are running well below capacity. Brent fell 5.85% to settle at $92.57 on Monday, WTI down to around $87.40, after Brent dropped 16% last week, its biggest weekly decline since the start of the Covid pandemic. Cheaper oil, if it holds, means lower fuel prices — but only if the diplomacy actually lands.

In short: Trump met the Qatari mediator on Monday, Iran's president says Tehran is ready to negotiate with dignity, but Rubio says no breakthrough is near and the two sides still disagree on whether nuclear talks come first — while oil plunged nearly 6% on hopes the standoff ends.

item.title: Anthropic and Meta both dropped new AI models on the same day
item.description:
Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on Monday, and Meta launched Muse Ember the same day — two very different bets on where AI goes next, one aimed at the hardest technical work, the other at making the routine work cheap.
Anthropic's release is the bigger of the two. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are the same underlying model, the company says, split by safeguards: Fable carries cybersecurity and biology blocks and is available to everyone on paid plans, Claude Code and the major cloud platforms, while Mythos drops some of those blocks and goes only to organisations approved through Anthropic's Cyber or Life Sciences Verification Programs. Anthropic says both are up to 30% faster than the 5.1 versions, communicate more clearly, and cost less — $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10/$50. On Anthropic's own benchmarks, Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% on the FrontierCode 2.0 agentic coding test, ahead of Opus 5.5 at 45.5%, and Artificial Analysis put it first on its Intelligence Index with a score of 65. Reuters notes the launch comes ahead of Anthropic's planned IPO — formal marketing of the shares to investors starts Tuesday, November 10, with a Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT. Cognition made Fable 5.2 available in its Devin coding tools on launch day.
Meta's Muse Ember goes the other way: the smallest and cheapest model in the Muse family, built for the repetitive work AI agents do all day — tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, pulling data out of long documents. It costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens, with a 1-million-token context window, and is live now on the Meta Model API and in Muse Code under the name muse-ember-1.0. Meta says Ember matches Anthropic's Claude Haiku 5.5 on Artificial Analysis's index at about a third of the cost per task — roughly $0.14 per task against Haiku's higher figure. But the comparison cuts both ways: on real coding tasks in FrontierCode 2.0, Haiku still wins, 34.9% to Ember's 27.2%. Ember's weights stay private, as with earlier Muse releases.
The two launches frame the same argument differently. Anthropic is selling capability at the top end — its most powerful model yet, with a restricted twin for vetted security and biology researchers, and a price cut to go with it. Meta is selling cost at the bottom end — near-Haiku intelligence for agent grunt work at a fraction of the price, betting that volume matters more than peak smarts. Both sets of benchmark claims are company-reported or from a single index, not independent validation, and both companies are racing OpenAI and Google, which have been releasing new models at a similar pace. For anyone who uses these tools, the practical effect is the same either way: faster, cheaper AI coding help, with Anthropic's top tier aimed at the most ambitious technical work and Meta's at the high-volume repetitive kind.
In short: Anthropic launched its most capable models yet — Fable 5.2 for everyone, Mythos 5.2 restricted to vetted security and life-sciences organisations — the day before its IPO roadshow starts, while Meta launched Muse Ember, a tiny model that matches Claude Haiku on one benchmark at about a third of the cost per task.
Sources: Reuters · MacRumors · SQ Magazine · The Hype · PYMNTS · Unite.AI · The Decoder
Note: posts circulating today about a "Claude Sonnet 4.6 launch" describe a release from February 2026, not a new model — not reported as news.
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Google's two new TPU systems take the Nvidia fight up a notch
item.description:
Google added two new systems to its eighth-generation TPU lineup on Monday — TPU 8tx for secure, confidential inference and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows — its fourth TPU system launch in a single year, and the clearest sign yet that Google intends its own chips to be a real alternative to Nvidia's.
The two systems solve different problems. TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the training-focused TPU 8t and paired with 5th-generation AMD EPYC hosts, builds security directly into the hardware layer: data and model weights stay encrypted and isolated even while in active use, which matters for governments and heavily regulated industries that currently have to unlock data in memory to process it. Google says it delivers up to 2x lower latency than TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. TPU 8i Max takes two existing TPU 8i chips and combines them into a single package, doubling compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth — built for the memory wall that appears when dozens of AI agents work across an entire codebase or hours of video at once. Both are expected to be available in 2027, according to Bloomberg; Google gave no prices or full specs.
The two sides of this race are Google's pitch and Nvidia's dominance. Google says it now has nearly 100 TPU customers — including Apple, Meta and Oracle, according to Bloomberg — that Anthropic has committed to 3.5 GW of TPU capacity starting in 2027, and that Oracle will offer TPUs through its cloud from next year. Every TPU Google has available is already contracted to a customer, the company says. Nvidia, meanwhile, still owns the AI accelerator market, and Google's own chip chief, Amin Vahdat, acknowledged the new systems are reconfigured versions of existing designs rather than new silicon. The bet is that packaging, security and software — Google also open-sourced TorchTPU and a TPU agent suite that plugs into Claude Code and Cursor — can win customers Nvidia's GPUs can't serve as cheaply.
For ordinary people the effect is indirect but real: the chips that train and run AI models are one of the biggest costs in the AI economy, and a genuine second supplier means cheaper AI services and less dependence on a single company. It also matters for the memory crunch Adam has been watching — Google is designing around the same memory wall that has pushed DRAM prices up 10–15% this quarter.
In short: Google launched two new TPU systems on Monday — the 8tx for hardware-level confidential computing and the 8i Max for huge context windows — bringing its 2026 total to four, with nearly 100 customers including Apple, Meta and Oracle, and both systems due in 2027.
Sources:
Source: storage.googleapis.com.

item.title: Nvidia — Commerce halted the Megaspeed probe after Nvidia's general counsel emailed investigators
item.description:
The New York Times reported Monday that the Commerce Department halted its months-long investigation into Megaspeed — the Singapore data-centre firm suspected of diverting billions of dollars of Nvidia AI chips to China — after Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter emailed the investigators in August 2025, saying senior Commerce official Jeff Kessler had given Nvidia permission to reach out.
The case was then transferred to the Justice Department, which is now running a criminal inquiry. Important caveat, stressed by several outlets relaying the Times report: the reporting does not establish that Nvidia's contact caused the halt — Kessler told the Times he did not direct investigators to share information with Nvidia, and a Commerce official said Kessler instructed them to proceed "by the book."
Nvidia's board investigation into CEO Jensen Huang continues; the House chairs want an answer by Wednesday, November 11, on a closed-door briefing November 18, and Nvidia reports Q3 earnings November 17. (NYT via WCCFTech · NYT via Clash Report · Superpower Daily)
Source: wccftech.com.

item.title: Houthi/Saudi — no new attacks Monday; Aramco Tower damage verified
item.description:
No new Houthi attacks were reported on Monday beyond the morning civil-defence alert in Riyadh, which was declared passed within minutes.
BBC Verify has now verified video showing windows blown out across several floors of the Aramco Tower in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District — more damage than the Energy Ministry's account of "minor damage" from falling debris suggested — though there were no casualties. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed two ballistic-missile launchers in Saada and Sanaa used in Sunday's attacks.
(Devdiscourse · Rigzone/Bloomberg · Media Pavilion)
Source: devdiscourse.com.

item.title: Khor Mor — Baghdad to supply household gas while the field stays shut
item.description:
Production at the Khor Mor gas field in Iraqi Kurdistan remained suspended on Monday while operator Dana Gas assesses damage from Sunday night's drone strike, which cut 2,500–2,800 MW — roughly 70–80% of the region's power.
New today: Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi ordered the federal Oil Ministry to supply the Kurdistan Region with liquefied petroleum gas until production resumes, and residents queued at filling stations on Monday, though officials in Sulaymaniyah said household gas stocks would last more than a month. No restart date has been given; after the November 2025 strike on the field, normal output was restored within a week.
No group has claimed responsibility — the 12th attack on the field since 2022. (The Insight International · Silent Dossier)
Source: theinsightinternational.com.

item.title: Israel — Eisenkot meets Lieberman; Knesset sworn in Tuesday
item.description:
Gadi Eisenkot met Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman on Monday to discuss who should head the opposition Change Bloc when the new Knesset is sworn in on Tuesday, with Eisenkot himself the most likely candidate.
Lieberman has ruled out supporting a government that depends on Arab parties, complicating Eisenkot's coalition arithmetic — his bloc holds 48 of 120 seats and needs 61. Netanyahu restated his vision for a unity government in a video statement on Monday.
Eisenkot has 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension. (Devdiscourse · Fact.net.in · JKN)
Source: devdiscourse.com.

item.title: Krakow — prosecutors say no ideology link established yet
item.description:
At a Monday briefing, National Prosecutor's Office spokesman Przemysław Nowak said investigators still lack evidence to tie gunman Michał Oksiński to any particular political ideology, despite Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński's earlier claim that he held radical ultranationalist views: "At the moment, we do not have elements that allow us to responsibly and categorically state that he was inspired by a particular ideology."
The terrorism classification stands, and the investigation into motive, accomplices and how he obtained 11 firearms legally through a shooting club continues. The first victim was named as Izabela Wozna, a 53-year-old artist and mother of four from Chodziez.
Wounded police officer Artur Morański underwent 12 hours of surgery. Post-mortems on all nine victims began Monday.
(Pollar · InfoHandle · RingkasNow)
Source: pollar.news.

item.title: CISA adds four exploited flaws to KEV — including "SSHole" — with a 3-day deadline
item.description:
CISA added four actively exploited vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Monday, with an unusually short federal deadline of November 12: CVE-2026-123158 ("SSHole"), the OpenSSH authentication bypass on musl-based Linux; CVE-2026-102895, a 9.8 improper-authentication flaw in GPUStack (open-source GPU cluster manager) observed exploited against a 2.1.1 deployment; CVE-2026-116779, a 9.8 code-injection flaw in SignalWire FreeSWITCH; and CVE-2026-123218, a 9.8 incorrect-authorisation flaw in IBM Aspera Faspex allowing an authenticated user to gain full admin privileges.
The catalog now stands at 1,773 entries. (CISA via CTXSec · Malice.ai)
Source: ctxsec.com.

item.title: "SSHole" is now confirmed exploited — hackers are breaking into Linux systems
item.description:
BleepingComputer reported Monday that hackers are actively exploiting the "SSHole" OpenSSH flaw (CVE-2026-123158) to execute commands, steal credentials and establish persistent access on Linux systems.
The flaw lets an attacker log in to accounts with no password on musl-based systems — Alpine Linux first of all — simply by entering a password longer than 256 characters. GreyNoise recorded the first successful exploitation in the wild on November 7, about 40 hours after the fix shipped, logging 16 successful attack chains from six source IPs; Previdian sensors confirmed 20 attempts from 13 IPs in nine countries.
WatchTowr said exploitation is associated with botnets and cryptomining. In one case, attackers gained root, changed DNS settings, started a hidden second SSH server and installed a remote-control agent with Chinese-language comments.
The fix is OpenSSH 10.6p2 (released November 5) or a distribution patch — or disable password authentication until patched. (BleepingComputer · Previdian)
Source: bleepingcomputer.com.

item.title: Fridge-hack spread across Europe, Guardian investigation finds
item.description:
A Guardian investigation published Sunday found the refrigeration-system attacks that hit French supermarkets last month also disrupted a London food wholesaler and retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden during the previous week.
French investigators are still hunting for those responsible, with no claim of responsibility; Sekoia has suggested a lone hacker may be behind it, possibly with no malware on the controllers at all. (Tech Current)
Source: teccurrent.com.

item.title: FTC v. Amazon — both sides move for summary judgment in the Prime case
item.description:
Amazon and the FTC have both moved for summary judgment in the Prime "dark patterns" case — Amazon seeking dismissal, the FTC seeking liability — after nearly two years of discovery. The FTC is seeking to hold three Amazon executives personally liable for potentially over $1 billion in penalties, alleging they knew about accidental Prime enrollments. At Friday's economics hearing in the separate antitrust case, Judge Chun pressed the FTC on what consumer harm it is actually trying to prove — lower quality, higher prices — and warned it to "keep an eye on" a similar consumer case he oversees that has been repeatedly dismissed. The Prime jury trial continues in Seattle. (Typefully · Typefully)
No fresh developments in the Netanyahu trial or the Murdaugh retrial (next hearing November 13).
Source: typefully.com.

New on the lists: MuJoCo 4.0, the robotics physics simulator's major release, with several breaking changes and Python 3.10 support dropped; anthropics/claude-quickstarts; and Anthropic's skills repository, whose Office document skills moved to Apache 2.0 on November 6. OpenMausBot has now shipped sixteen releases since October 30.

(Daily Diff · GitDiscover · LuonG NV · FindaRepo)

item.title: Ukraine hits Russia's second-biggest refinery as Moscow blacks out 12 regions — on the eve of Abu Dhabi talks
item.description:
Ukrainian drones set fire to Russia's second-largest oil refinery overnight, and Russian missiles and drones knocked out power across 12 Ukrainian regions, in a final round of energy strikes the day before US-mediated talks open in Abu Dhabi. Both sides arrived at the negotiating table having just demonstrated they can still hit each other's energy infrastructure at will.
The Ukrainian strike hit the KINEF refinery at Kirishi, in Russia's Leningrad region about 800 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. The regional governor, Alexander Drozdenko, confirmed drones struck the town's industrial zone and a fire broke out at the refinery, which he described as Russia's second-largest, processing around 400,000 barrels a day — about 20 million tonnes a year, more than 6% of Russia's refined output. Independent Russian outlet ASTRA confirmed from local video that the fire was at the refinery itself, and NASA's FIRMS satellite system registered multiple heat hotspots at the site, the Kyiv Independent reported. Drozdenko said air defences downed 113 Ukrainian drones over the region during the attack — his count rose from 81 while the operation was still under way, according to TASS — and a woman was killed in the town of Vsevolozhsk when drone debris struck the roof of her apartment building. An apartment in Kirishi was also damaged and a family evacuated. The fire was contained, the governor said, but the extent of damage to the plant's processing units has not been independently confirmed, and the operator has not commented. The refinery has been hit before — in May, strikes damaged three of its four crude distillation units, and again on August 30.
Russia's reply was a large overnight barrage of its own. President Zelenskyy said it involved more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones, and Ukraine's Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said consumers were left without electricity in 12 regions: Vinnytsia, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Odesa, Poltava, Rivne, Kharkiv, Khmelnytskyi and Chernihiv. Nekrasov said the situation was most difficult in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kyiv regions. Ukraine's energy ministry accused Russia of deliberately targeting the energy and oil and gas sectors 128 times over the past week, with 219 incidents of damage or destruction recorded. Russia's defence ministry said it had struck three electricity substations, and claimed to have hit a cargo ship in the Black Sea it said was carrying weapons to Ukraine — a claim with no independent confirmation. Meanwhile the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant, which lost all external power on Sunday for the 27th time in the war, is back on the grid after about ten hours on diesel generators — but through the same single 330-kV line that keeps failing, with its main 750-kV line still down since October 23, according to the IAEA.
The two sides tell the story of this energy war very differently. Kyiv says it never formally agreed to the energy ceasefire President Trump announced unilaterally in October, and senior Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent it was never a deal — though Zelenskyy has said Ukraine would halt refinery strikes if Russia stopped hitting energy targets. Moscow, for its part, presents its strikes as retaliation and has accused Kyiv of contradicting US peace efforts. Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for contributing to higher diesel and gasoline prices in the United States, although he has also acknowledged that his decision to attack Iran alongside Israel played a major role in the increase — and rising fuel costs contributed to Republican losses in last week's midterm elections.
The talks themselves open Tuesday, November 10, in Abu Dhabi, running two days. Reuters reports that Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will lead the US side, France's foreign minister said Europeans will be represented, and Russia's delegation is reported to be led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky. Ukraine's priorities, according to the Associated Press, are halting strikes on energy facilities and critical infrastructure, resuming grain shipments through the Black Sea, and expanding prisoner exchanges. It is the fourth round sponsored by the Trump administration, after the last round in Geneva in February, and previous rounds have made no tangible progress toward ending the war.
For ordinary people, the human cost is measured in cold and dark: hundreds of thousands without power in Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions alone, emergency and scheduled outages across most of Ukraine, and a refinery fire 800 kilometres inside Russia that shows nowhere in either country's energy system is out of reach. The 48 hours before the talks brought a massive Russian strike on Ukraine's power system and Ukrainian strikes on Kirishi and Rostov in return — the agenda for Abu Dhabi is being written by the attacks themselves.
In short: Ukraine set Russia's second-largest refinery on fire overnight while Russian strikes blacked out 12 Ukrainian regions, and both sides head into Tuesday's Abu Dhabi talks having shown they can still hit each other's energy infrastructure — with Kyiv saying it never agreed to an energy ceasefire in the first place.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Iran talks are frozen, both sides say — but the backchannel is still moving
item.description:
A day after President Trump told CNN that fresh US strikes on Iran were "highly unlikely" if talks keep progressing, both Washington and Tehran are now saying the talks themselves have stalled — while quietly keeping the backchannel alive through Qatar.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Qatari mediators in New York on Monday to discuss Tehran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. He told Iranian state media the Qataris would carry the ideas discussed to the US side and that he hoped to receive Washington's final response by Tuesday, then said he would fly back to Tehran within hours: "Whenever the Qataris have a response, they know how to get it to us." The Iranian plan, announced Friday at the UN General Assembly, calls on the US to release frozen Iranian funds, lift sanctions and end its naval blockade of Iranian ports — steps Araghchi said could be completed within four or five days, allowing the strait to reopen and negotiations on a final agreement, including on Iran's nuclear programme, to begin by the seventh day. Trump rejected the proposal on Saturday, calling it "unacceptable."
Washington's public answer came from Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said on Sunday he could not say the two sides were "on the verge of a breakthrough" and called Tehran's demands "unacceptable," "outrageous" and "ridiculous." A US official told Al Jazeera the indirect discussions were "positive and constructive" but stressed there would be no agreement unless Iran's nuclear programme is addressed, adding that Trump is willing to relieve sanctions and release frozen funds in exchange for progress on nuclear issues. The official said Iran has indicated flexibility on the nuclear questions, but the sides remain apart on timing and who moves first — and expressed scepticism of Tehran, saying it broke the memorandum of understanding signed in June by firing on commercial vessels. Tehran denies that and says Washington broke its commitments by failing to halt Israel's attacks on Lebanon and by seeking alternate shipping routes through the strait.
The two sides' versions of the stall do not agree on the cause. Araghchi said on Sunday that mediators had made no progress since the "shock" of the US midterm elections and that it would take time for the atmosphere to become conducive to visits resuming. Rubio, speaking before flying to Paris for the G7 foreign ministers' meeting, dismissed suggestions a deal is imminent while acknowledging that multiple third-party nations are mediating. Behind the public statements, Vice President J.D. Vance has been speaking almost daily with mediators, including Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani and Pakistan's military chief Asim Munir, and Qatari officials are expected to continue discussions in Tehran on Tuesday. Trump is meeting the Qatari prime minister at the White House on Monday, and told reporters Monday: "We're going to win. It's going to go pretty quickly," adding that gas prices would fall once the US won the war. In Tehran, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei struck a defiant tone, saying the days of foreign domination were over, while Iran's armed forces chief warned of a "decisive and devastating response" to any threat.
For the world economy, the shipping war is the part that bites. Iran closed the strait — which handled roughly 20% of the world's oil and gas before the war — shortly after the US and Israel launched their offensive on February 28, and flows are running well below capacity. Crude exports from major Middle East producers rebounded in September to 12.8 million barrels a day, their highest since the war began, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters — but still far below February's 18.8 million. Brent fell 1.7% to $96.67 a barrel on Monday morning, with WTI at $89.87, after Brent dropped 16% last week, its biggest weekly decline since the start of the Covid pandemic. The US has also imposed a blockade on Iranian ports and threatened secondary sanctions against airports and companies doing business with Iranian airlines; the UAE, Iraq and Oman have already cancelled related flights. Iran's navy claimed on Sunday that a fourth tanker had struck a mine in the strait — a claim Reuters could not confirm, and one that conflicts with the Revolutionary Guards' own count of three.
In short: both sides now say the Iran talks are stalled — Araghchi blames the post-midterm freeze, Rubio calls Tehran's demands ridiculous — but the Qatari backchannel is still running, with a US answer expected by Tuesday, Qatari officials heading to Tehran, and Trump meeting the Qatari prime minister today. Oil fell again on Monday as traders bet the standoff holds.
Sources:
Source: aljazeeranews-mggx1uo47w.edgeone.app.

item.title: Krakow gunman dies in hospital before he can be questioned
item.description:
The 24-year-old suspected of killing six people in Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday — and, investigators believe, his parents and sister earlier the same day — died in hospital early on Monday, taking whatever motive he had with him. He had never been questioned, and now never will be.
The man, identified by Polish media as Michał O., died at approximately 4.30am on Monday, according to Krzysztof Klęczar, the governor of the Małopolska region. He had undergone at least three operations after being critically wounded in a shootout with police on Saturday, and prosecutors had been unable to question him because of his condition. Eryk Stasielak, a prosecutor at Poland's National Prosecutor's Office, said proceedings directly concerning the deceased suspect would be discontinued, but the wider inquiry — including whether anyone else knew about his plans — will continue. Post-mortem examinations of all nine victims began on Monday and could take about two days.
The dead are now counted as ten including the gunman: six in the Main Market Square — a 51-year-old Austrian woman, a 32-year-old British man, three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man of about 50 — and three at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometres north-east of Krakow: his 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and younger sister, all with gunshot wounds. Fifteen other people were wounded, including two police officers — one stable, one serious but stable. The officer who arrested the attacker was woken from an induced coma on Sunday.
What investigators do know is piecemeal. Police recovered 11 firearms from locations connected to the shootings, including seven at the family property — a total matching the number of weapons covered by permits held by the suspect and his father. Michał O. held a valid firearms licence, had no previous criminal convictions and was not previously known to police, and some weapons had been positioned within reach of the driver's seat of his Subaru. Officers found no letter or other document on the suspect or inside his car explaining his actions, though they are analysing his phone, electronic storage devices and handwritten notes. Interior ministry spokeswoman Karolina Gałecka told Polish radio on Monday that specialists were still examining emblems and patches found on the suspect's clothing.
The two sides of the motive question are, for now, one official reading and no answer. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect held radical ultranationalist views and appeared fascinated by far-right ideologies, and Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the shooting an act of terrorism. The National Prosecutor's Office formally classified the attack as a suspected terrorist offence on Sunday. But the authorities have not established whether the gunman's political beliefs directly motivated the killings, no evidence of membership of an organised extremist group has been publicly disclosed, and Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said investigators had obtained evidence that could help explain the events but declined to disclose its contents. Le Monde reports that disinformation about the attacker's political affiliations spread from Saturday night into Sunday.
For Krakow, the human picture is mourning, not answers. Poland declared two days of national mourning on November 8–9, running through November 11 in Krakow, and residents and visitors have placed flowers and candles near the square, which reopened to the public on Sunday evening. The investigation now becomes a reconstruction — the full sequence, the source of the weapons, the meaning of the emblems, and whether anyone else took part in planning — carried out without the one person who could have explained it.
In short: the Krakow gunman died in hospital at 4.30am on Monday, never having been questioned, so the investigation into nine murders — six in the square, three at his family home — now has to be rebuilt from forensics, phones and witnesses, with a suspected far-right motive still unproven and no note or letter left behind.
Sources:
Source: nexuseuropa.eu.

item.title: Russell Brand jailed for 10 and a half years for rape and sexual assault
item.description:
Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after a jury convicted him last week of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three more. The 51-year-old comedian was sentenced at London's Southwark Crown Court on Monday morning, and showed no emotion as the sentence was read out.
Judge Joel Bennathan handed down nine years for the count of rape and 18 months for the three sexual assault charges — nine, 18 and eight months respectively — running consecutively, for a total of 10 years and six months. Brand must serve two-thirds of the sentence before he is eligible for parole, according to the Guardian — meaning at least seven years behind bars. The judge told him he was a sexual predator who believed that "fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live," and that he had shown a "casual, arrogant disregard of any woman's right to say no to you." He added: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and demand justice in the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Mr Brand, act without their consent." As Brand left the dock he mouthed "I love you" to his wife, Laura Brand, and told her "we'll be ok" as he was taken away.
The conviction came on Thursday, November 5, after a trial lasting around four weeks that began on October 12. The jury convicted Brand on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and acquitted him on two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. The offences the jury found him guilty of were committed against four women between 2004 and 2009, at locations including a radio station, the set of a DVD recording and Brand's home; the wider allegations heard at trial spanned 1999 to 2009 and involved six women. Brand pleaded not guilty throughout, testified that he never had non-consensual sex and that he believed "consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and in many ways, more important than sex itself," and said he had "misused" his fame to have sexual encounters with women. His defence argued the 2023 documentary that brought the allegations to light had sparked a wave of false accusations, and that "the well of justice had been corrupted and contaminated."
The two sides of the case could hardly be further apart — and the jury sided with the prosecution. Prosecutors told the court Brand was a "predator" who used his fame to sleep with women and didn't care if they consented or not. Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, of the Metropolitan Police, said after the verdict that the outcome was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward," and added: "Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be." Victim impact statements were read in court before sentencing on Monday. The case began with a September 2023 joint investigation by Channel 4's *Dispatches*, the Sunday Times and the Times; police gathered evidence from more than 100 witnesses, took over 400 witness statements and reviewed more than 1,400 documents.
For the women involved, and for the wider question of what fame protects, the sentence is the end of one case but not of the police work: the Metropolitan Police said its investigation into rape allegations made by two more women remains ongoing, including one involving a woman who was 16 at the time, and files have been submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service. Brand was remanded into custody after the verdict and has been held at HMP Wandsworth.
In short: Russell Brand, 51, was jailed for 10 and a half years on Monday after being convicted of one rape and three sexual assaults against four women between 2004 and 2009 — the judge called him a sexual predator who believed fame put him above the rules, and he must serve at least seven years before parole. Police are still investigating allegations from two more women.
Sources:
Source: usatoday.com.

The case began with a September 2023 joint investigation by Channel 4's *Dispatches*, the Sunday Times and the Times; police gathered evidence from more than 100 witnesses, took over 400 witness statements and reviewed more than 1,400 documents.

For the women involved, and for the wider question of what fame protects, the sentence is the end of one case but not of the police work: the Metropolitan Police said its investigation into rape allegations made by two more women remains ongoing, including one involving a woman who was 16 at the time, and files have been submitted to the Crown Prosecution Service. Brand was remanded into custody after the verdict and has been held at HMP Wandsworth.

In short: Russell Brand, 51, was jailed for 10 and a half years on Monday after being convicted of one rape and three sexual assaults against four women between 2004 and 2009 — the judge called him a sexual predator who believed fame put him above the rules, and he must serve at least seven years before parole. Police are still investigating allegations from two more women.

item.title: Houthi/Saudi — Monday alert in Riyadh, no new strikes reported
item.description:
Saudi civil defence raised an alert in Riyadh on Monday morning and declared the danger passed minutes later, a day after Houthi missiles damaged the Aramco Tower in the capital's financial district.
BBC Verify has now verified video showing windows blown out across several floors of the tower — more damage than the Energy Ministry's account of "minor damage" from falling debris suggested — though there were no casualties. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed ballistic-missile launchers in Saada and Sanaa that it said were used in Sunday's attacks, after intercepting three ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles.
No new Houthi attacks were reported on Monday beyond the morning alert. (Devdiscourse · OE Digital)
Source: devdiscourse.com.
