item.title: Khor Mor gas field drone attack blacks out most of Iraqi Kurdistan
item.description:
A drone struck a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank at the Khor Mor gas field in Iraq's Kurdistan region late on Sunday night, setting off a fire, halting all production and knocking out 2,500–2,800 megawatts of generation — roughly 70–80% of the region's electricity.
Gas supply was cut to power plants serving Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, a population of five to six million, with hospitals and water stations given priority and supply projected at five to six hours a day in places. Operator Dana Gas confirmed on Monday that the fire was out but production remains suspended pending a damage assessment, with no restart timetable.
Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment found no casualties and ordered a joint investigation. No group has claimed responsibility — the 12th attack on the field since 2022 — though Kurdish officials have previously blamed Iran-aligned Iraqi armed groups for earlier strikes on the region's energy sites, and Iraqi security sources said the drone approached from the direction of Tuz Khurmatu, outside Kurdistan's control.
The field, run by the Pearl Petroleum consortium, supplies more than 80% of Kurdistan's electricity. Developing — attribution and restart date both open.
(Business Times via Reuters · Silent Dossier · Political.org)
Source: btin.co.in.

item.title: Israel — Eisenkot reaches out to Netanyahu's allies; Knesset sworn in Tuesday
item.description:
Gadi Eisenkot has begun his 28-day mandate by reaching out to Benjamin Netanyahu's allies — appealing to Likud and to Religious Zionism to join a national emergency government under him as prime minister — while his own bloc holds only 48 of the 120 Knesset seats and needs 61.
Avigdor Liberman is willing to compromise on conscription to build a 61-seat government without Arab parties, and Eisenkot himself is said to prefer a 48-seat minority government with Arab parties supporting from outside, with the ultra-Orthodox possibly abstaining. His four conditions for partners stand: recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, commitment to the Declaration of Independence, universal national or civil service, and designating Hamas a terrorist organisation.
The new Knesset is sworn in on Tuesday, November 10. (Lanka Leader/Reuters · Particle)
Source: lankaleader.lk.

item.title: Chainalysis breach was far worse than first disclosed — credentials and live tokens for all users exposed
item.description:
Chainalysis has confirmed that names, usernames, password hashes and live authentication tokens for all of its users were exposed to a malicious actor — a much wider disclosure than its October 30 statement, which said it had found no evidence that credentials or session tokens had been touched.
The company added the sentence to its incident notice late on Wednesday, November 4, and told some customers an "on-path attack" had exposed a subset of passwords. The attack used what the company calls "offensive agentic techniques."
As of its November 7 update, Reactor, KYT and Address Screening are back online with tighter controls — customers must submit trusted IPs for an allowlist, reset passwords and rotate API keys — while Data Solutions and Chain (Beta) are still offline. No user count has been given, and the company has not answered questions about why the wider exposure was disclosed days after it was discovered.
For anyone in crypto compliance, this is the firm police and banks call when crypto goes missing — and its own login and screening tools were the ones hit. (Tech Insider · Netics Labs)
Source: tech-insider.org.

item.title: No new CISA KEV additions; "sshole" OpenSSH flaw now has sensor exploitation evidence
item.description:
CISA has added nothing new to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog since the SonicWall SonicOS flaw (CVE-2026-19868) on November 6 — the catalog stands at 1,769 entries, federal deadline November 20.
TheHackerNews' November 9 write-up adds that SonicWall also patched other high-severity SonicOS flaws in the same round, including CVE-2026-107155 (8.8) and CVE-2026-82308 (7.5). Separately, the "sshole" OpenSSH flaw (CVE-2026-123158) now has direct sensor-exploitation evidence from GreyNoise dated November 7, after the first real exploit attempts on November 5 — still no confirmed production victims.
(The Hacker News · The Disruption Continuum)
Source: thehackernews.com.

item.title: The "Apple taps Google Gemini" stories dated today are stale
item.description:
The Apple–Google deal — Gemini models and cloud tech as the basis for the next generation of Apple Foundation Models, powering a more personalised Siri — was announced in January 2026, not today. Pieces carrying today's date are republications of that announcement. Not new, not reported as news.
Apple's agentic-Siri push (Gurman/Bloomberg, covered last night) and Google's K-12 Search/Gemini opt-in (covered November 3–4) have no fresh developments this morning.

item.title: Nvidia's board opens an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over an alleged Chinese spy link
item.description:
Nvidia's board of directors announced on Sunday that it is opening an independent investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation — hours after Huang told employees in an email that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Huang, 63, remains CEO while the inquiry runs, and the board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised. It is the biggest corporate-governance story in tech this year, landing the night before Huang's GTC keynote and nine days before Nvidia's quarterly earnings.
The woman at the centre of the reports is Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le — not related to Jensen Huang — a former executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based data-centre company and major Nvidia customer in Southeast Asia. According to the New York Times, US intelligence agencies concluded last year that she was sharing information with the Chinese government while working with Nvidia to build data centres in Asia, and a highly classified spring 2025 memo warned top Trump administration officials that she had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to learn about US-made AI chips and possibly push Nvidia to make its most advanced chips available in China. The Financial Times later reported that a US intelligence memo alleged a romantic relationship between the two Huangs. Megaspeed has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips since June 2024, according to the Times, and officials from the Commerce and Justice departments have been investigating Megaspeed and its potential ties to the Chinese government for more than a year. Megaspeed was spun off from a Chinese company in 2023.
Huang's email to staff, reported by CNBC and others, said he had been unfaithful to his wife, that his actions had hurt her and their children, and that he took full responsibility. He apologised to colleagues and shareholders, said he remained committed to leading Nvidia, and asked for privacy for his family. "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports," he wrote, "Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation." The board said a committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent lawyers, will oversee the review, and that Huang supports it and has committed to cooperating. It gave no timetable. The Wall Street Journal reports that Huang will remain CEO while the inquiry proceeds, and Bloomberg reported the same.
The two sides of this story disagree sharply on what the relationship meant. US officials cited by the Journal and the Times treat Alice Huang as a recruited intelligence asset who used the relationship to get close to the head of the world's most important AI chipmaker. China's Foreign Ministry has called the allegations "unsubstantiated" and described them as smears. Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs said its officials had not claimed Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset and had not investigated her personally — though it confirmed an investigation into Megaspeed is ongoing. Nvidia previously described Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang as "not unusual or unexpected" given their business ties, and Huang told Bloomberg the company had examined Megaspeed's GPU deployments and found no evidence its chips had been illegally diverted to China. An affair admission does not establish that Huang knowingly assisted an intelligence operation or disclosed sensitive information — that is exactly what the board inquiry is meant to examine.
Congress is moving in parallel. Three Republican House committee chairs — Brian Mast (Foreign Affairs), John Moolenaar (China Select) and Rick Crawford (Intelligence) — have asked Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on November 18 about his interactions with Alice Huang and Nvidia's protections against foreign espionage, and to accept the date or propose an alternative by November 11. Senator Elizabeth Warren cited reporting that Megaspeed had bought at least $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia chips.
For ordinary people the stakes are less about the affair than about the chips. Nvidia sits at the centre of the US-China AI race, and its hardware powers much of the AI boom — the same boom that has already pushed up memory prices and reshaped tech spending. Markets have not yet had a chance to react: the announcement came on a Sunday, so Monday's open is the first test, and Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on November 17. Huang is still scheduled to deliver the GTC keynote on Monday at 9 a.m. CET, which now lands hours after the board's announcement.
In short: Nvidia's board is independently investigating whether its CEO was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation, after Huang admitted to an affair with a Megaspeed executive US intelligence agencies suspect of passing information to Beijing. The board says it has no evidence secrets were compromised, Huang stays in charge, and Congress wants him briefed by November 18 — with markets, the GTC keynote and earnings all coming in the next nine days.
Sources:
Source: dexerto.com.

item.title: Iran talks stall after the midterms — Araghchi warns of "hell" if the US chooses war
item.description:
Hours after President Trump told CNN on Sunday that fresh US strikes on Iran were "highly unlikely" if talks keep progressing, Iran's foreign minister said the talks themselves have gone quiet — and warned Washington to accept Tehran's offer or face military retaliation. Both sides are now publicly saying the diplomacy has stalled, and blaming each other for it.
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X on Sunday: "American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own." He said Iran's two-day proposal still stands — under it, the US would end the war on all fronts, unfreeze Iranian assets, lift oil sanctions and end its naval blockade of Iranian ports, and Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days. "Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell," he added. Speaking to reporters in Tehran, he said mediators had made no progress since the "shock" of the US midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. "The main reason is the US election results, which have obviously come as a shock to everyone," Araghchi said, according to Al Jazeera. "It will take some time for things to settle down and for the atmosphere to become conducive to the mediators resuming their visits. We have to wait."
Washington's answer, delivered Sunday by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, was equally blunt. Speaking to reporters at Homestead Air Reserve Base in Florida before flying to Paris for the G7 foreign ministers' meeting, Rubio said diplomatic efforts had achieved no breakthrough and called Tehran's demands "unacceptable," "outrageous" and "ridiculous," according to ANI, citing Al Jazeera. He acknowledged that multiple third-party nations are mediating, but dismissed suggestions a deal is imminent. His assessment lines up with Araghchi's on one point — nothing is moving — and clashes with Qatar's statement on Saturday that "significant progress" had been made.
Behind the public statements, the backchannel is still alive. EA WorldView reports that Vice President J.D. Vance has been speaking almost daily with mediators, including Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani and Pakistan's military chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, and that the two sides have discussed a working-level technical meeting in the coming days. Iranian negotiators are reviewing proposals to limit Tehran's nuclear programme, according to a US official and a diplomat cited by EA WorldView, and Qatari officials are expected to continue discussions in Tehran on Tuesday. Vance has said the Iran war was a leading cause of the Democrats' midterm victories.
The US is also tightening the economic screws. Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein told Al Jazeera that the US Treasury has asked Baghdad to shut almost all of its commercial border crossings with Iran, leaving only two operational — one of them in the autonomous Kurdistan region. Hussein said the Hormuz blockade has already cost Iraq $60 billion, and that backchannel agreements had previously let Iraqi crude move through the strait via a designated southerly corridor. Fighting has largely subsided, AFP reports, but Iran is still trying to blockade the strait while the US Navy maintains its counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
The two sides remain far apart on sequencing, and that is the core of the stall. Washington insists nuclear issues must feature in the first talks; Tehran says it will not negotiate on its atomic programme until its core conditions are addressed. Trump has said he is willing to relieve sanctions and release frozen funds in exchange for progress on nuclear issues, but on Sunday he also repeated that he would strike again "if necessary" — and named 38 bridges the US could knock down in an hour.
For the world economy, the shipping war is the part that bites: flows through Hormuz are running at under 60% of capacity, and Brent settled around $98 on Friday after a roughly 12% weekly drop. For Iraq, a country that depends on oil exports, the blockade is already a $60 billion wound. And for the region, the next watch points are concrete: whether mediator travel resumes, whether Qatari officials' Tuesday talks in Tehran produce anything, and whether the new moon on Monday — a dark night favourable for military operations — brings any movement. The US carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt is not expected in the region before mid-November.
In short: a day after Trump took new strikes off the table, Iran says mediation has frozen since the midterms and warns of "hell" if Washington chooses war, while Rubio calls Tehran's demands ridiculous and says there is no breakthrough. The backchannel through Vance and the Qataris is still open, with talks in Tehran on Tuesday, but both sides are now publicly dug in — and the US is squeezing Iraq's border trade with Iran in the meantime.
Sources:
Source: aapnews.imgdeliver.net.

Trump has said he is willing to relieve sanctions and release frozen funds in exchange for progress on nuclear issues, but on Sunday he also repeated that he would strike again "if necessary" — and named 38 bridges the US could knock down in an hour.

For the world economy, the shipping war is the part that bites: flows through Hormuz are running at under 60% of capacity, and Brent settled around $98 on Friday after a roughly 12% weekly drop. For Iraq, a country that depends on oil exports, the blockade is already a $60 billion wound. And for the region, the next watch points are concrete: whether mediator travel resumes, whether Qatari officials' Tuesday talks in Tehran produce anything, and whether the new moon on Monday — a dark night favourable for military operations — brings any movement. The US carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt is not expected in the region before mid-November.

In short: a day after Trump took new strikes off the table, Iran says mediation has frozen since the midterms and warns of "hell" if Washington chooses war, while Rubio calls Tehran's demands ridiculous and says there is no breakthrough. The backchannel through Vance and the Qataris is still open, with talks in Tehran on Tuesday, but both sides are now publicly dug in — and the US is squeezing Iraq's border trade with Iran in the meantime.

item.title: Russian drone hit rescue crews at the Komyshuvakha aid-centre site
item.description:
A Russian drone struck emergency workers on Sunday at the site of the November 2 bombing of a humanitarian aid centre in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, damaging specialised rescue equipment.
No one was injured in the strike, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service, but it came as crews were still searching for victims of an attack that has now killed at least 55 people, with around 45–50 still listed as missing by Ukraine's military intelligence agency, HUR. Ukraine has accused Russia of a "double tap" — a second strike aimed at the rescuers responding to the first.
President Zelenskyy condemned the strike as an example of "extreme brutality." The toll of 55 was already reported; the strike on the rescue crews is new.
(Bytes Europe/AP · EuropeSays)
Source: byteseu.com.

item.title: Main Market Square reopens; post-mortems start Monday
item.description:
Krakow's Main Market Square reopened to residents and tourists on Sunday evening, a day after the shooting that killed six people and wounded 15.
Post-mortem examinations on all nine victims — the six killed in Krakow and the suspect's parents and sister in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski — begin on Monday morning and are likely to continue into Tuesday, prosecutor Eryk Stasielak told the Polish Press Agency. The 24-year-old suspect, Michał O., remains in critical condition, and prosecutors will decide on Monday what steps to take involving him if he survives.
The investigation into the six Krakow killings and the three deaths at the family home is being handled as one case, classified as an act of a terrorist nature. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect acted alone and held radical, ultra-nationalist views; Le Monde reports that disinformation about the attacker's political affiliations spread from Saturday night into Sunday.
Of the two wounded police officers, one is stable and the other is serious but stable. (Energy Radio · Le Monde)
Source: energyradio.uk.

item.title: Apple is pushing to make Siri truly agentic — as early as next year
item.description:
Apple CEO John Ternus has pressed software chief Craig Federighi to move past Siri tweaks, with an autonomous, agentic Siri targeted as early as next year, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports.
Gurman says the closed-door meeting happened in recent weeks, that Apple's internal comparison set is ChatGPT Dots, Meta's Muse and Grok, and that Apple is reworking how it develops iOS, iPadOS and macOS 28 to give engineers more room before features lock. Fine-grained control of Apple's own apps — rotating and cropping photos in Photos, organising Safari tabs — is expected with iOS 27.3.
Gurman reports Apple has no illusions about keeping pace with its rivals. Single-source (Gurman/Bloomberg), so treat the timeline as reported, not confirmed.
(Daily AI Thread · FourWeekMBA)
Source: dailyaithread.com.

item.title: Anthropic's IPO filing: $895 billion in compute commitments (catch-up, Nov 2)
item.description:
Anthropic's amended IPO filing (S-1/A, November 2) discloses about $895.4 billion in purchase commitments and lease agreements, nearly all of it for computing power and data centres — more than double the $430 billion in its original October filing.
About $69.8 billion falls due in the next 12 months, and $447.5 billion by the end of 2030. The filing also adds Q3 results: about $17 billion in revenue (up 12x year over year) and a $567 million operating loss.
The biggest suppliers: Broadcom (~$161 billion in equipment leases), Google (~$121 billion), SpaceX's AI unit (up to $120.5 billion) and Amazon (~$110 billion). The roadshow can start November 10 at the earliest.
Why it matters: it puts a hard number on what frontier AI actually costs to run — and how much of that bill comes due before the revenue to pay for it. (Unite.AI · AI Intent)
Source: unite.ai.

item.title: Japanese retailer Iris Ohyama: data of up to 7.7 million people may be exposed in a cloud breach
item.description:
Japanese manufacturer Iris Ohyama, which runs the Iris Plaza online store, disclosed that personal information belonging to about 7.7 million people may have been exposed after unauthorised access to a third-party cloud service it uses.
The company found a suspicious file in the external cloud service on October 28, suspended Iris Plaza and related systems, and disclosed the incident on October 29. The potentially exposed data covers about 5.8 million registered and former members plus 1.9 million non-members — names, addresses, phone numbers and birthdates; some passwords were encrypted, and credit card information was not stored in the affected service.
The company says it has not confirmed how many records were actually accessed, has received no reports of misuse as of November 5, and has not identified the attackers or received any direct communication from them. Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission and police were notified October 29.
(BleepingComputer · Neowin)
Source: bleepingcomputer.com.

item.description:

SANS Internet Storm Center honeypots saw long-password exploit attempts rise from 23 on November 1 to 713 on November 6, with the first real exploit attempts on November 5. If you run an internet-facing SSH server, this is one to patch and watch.

item.title: Eisenkot's coalition puzzle: two rival plans take shape
item.description:
With the Knesset sworn in on Tuesday, November 10, the two rival coalition plans are now clear. Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman says he is willing to compromise on conscription legislation and wants a government of 61 MKs without the Arab parties, bringing in all of United Torah Judaism and Shas. Eisenkot's alternative is a minority government of his 48-seat bloc, supported externally by the Arab parties, potentially with United Torah Judaism abstaining. Negotiating teams from Yisrael Beiteinu and Yashar met minutes after Liberman's announcement, and Eisenkot and Liberman are expected to meet despite their rivalry. Eisenkot wants to move fast; Liberman expects a slower process. (Israel RealTime · Votendi)
No fresh developments: Russell Brand's sentencing is Monday, November 9; FTC v. Amazon, the Netanyahu trial and the Murdaugh retrial (next hearing November 13) are all quiet.
Source: israelrealtime.com.

item.title: Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant loses all external power — then gets it back the same day
item.description:
Europe's largest nuclear power plant spent most of Sunday running on emergency diesel generators after losing its last external power line in the early hours, the UN's nuclear watchdog said — the 27th time the plant has lost all off-site power since the war began. By evening, Ukraine's state nuclear operator Energoatom said the line had been switched back on at 17:41, reconnecting the plant to the grid.
The outage began at 02:36 on Sunday, when the Ferosplavna-1 line — a 330 kV link and the plant's only remaining grid connection — disconnected. An automatic reconnection attempt failed, leaving the plant's own systems supplied solely by backup diesel generators. The International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed the outage and said the cause and location of the disconnection were not yet known. The Russian-installed plant management said automatic protection systems had shut the line down after damage was detected, and that radiation levels on site and in the surrounding zone were normal.
All six of the plant's reactors are shut down, but the fuel in them still needs continuous cooling — and cooling needs electricity. The IAEA said the plant had enough diesel to run a limited number of emergency generators for about two weeks. Energoatom warned that operating in blackout mode "creates a direct risk of failure of life-support systems and nuclear fuel cooling in the event that diesel generators break down or exhaust their fuel reserves, which could lead to a radiation accident." IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi called for the grid connection to be restored and diesel stocks increased. The plant's other main line, Dniprovska, has been unavailable since at least October 23, and in a November 6 update the IAEA said work was still needed to reconnect it — so the site was down to a single line before Sunday's failure, and it still is.
The blackout came on top of another night of Russian strikes on Ukraine's grid. DTEK, the country's largest private energy company, said the overnight attack left more than 600,000 people without power in the Dnipropetrovsk region, and national grid operator Ukrenergo imposed emergency power cuts in Kharkiv, Sumy and Poltava. Russia's defence ministry said on Sunday it had also hit a power substation in the Zhytomyr region and three cargo vessels in the Black Sea that it claimed were supporting Ukraine's military — claims Kyiv has not confirmed. Zelenskyy has accused Moscow of intensifying the energy campaign to pressure Kyiv ahead of trilateral talks with Russia and the United States in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10–11. Moscow says it is striking military-industrial, energy and transport targets.
For ordinary Ukrainians the stakes are immediate: temperatures in Kyiv are near freezing, emergency and scheduled outages are running across most regions, and Kyiv's water supply was only just restored after its worst outage of the war. For the wider region, the Zaporizhzhia blackout is the sharper warning — a plant with no grid connection and a two-week diesel clock, in a war zone, for the 27th time.
In short: Zaporizhzhia lost its last power line early Sunday and ran on diesel generators for most of the day before power was restored in the evening — but with its backup line still down, the plant remains one failure from another blackout, while Russian strikes left 600,000+ people without power in Dnipropetrovsk alone, two days before the Abu Dhabi talks.
Sources:
Source: thehindubusinessline.com.

item.title: Trump says new Iran strikes "highly unlikely" if talks progress — but names 38 bridges as targets
item.description:
President Trump told CNN on Sunday that he is "highly unlikely" to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the conflict keep progressing — the clearest signal yet that the post-midterm escalation he had hinted at may not come. "It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement," he said in a phone interview with CNN's Jim Sciutto. "The answer is, highly unlikely it's going to be necessary."
The reassurance came with a threat attached. Trump said that if strikes do resume, the US has already identified potential infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges "that we can knock down in literally one hour." He also said Iran was "withering away" financially and militarily, and that US forces in the region are prepared to strike at any moment. "I would, if necessary," he said.
Tehran's response on Sunday was to press its own case. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the midterm results should push the White House to accept Iran's two-day proposal to end the war — under which Washington would lift its blockade of Iranian ports, agree a ceasefire on all fronts and unfreeze Iranian assets, and Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days. Araghchi has spoken to 12 foreign ministers in 48 hours, and Iran submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar on Thursday. The seven conditions Tehran has set — sanctions relief, frozen assets, war reparations and an end to the blockade among them — still stand, and Iran insists the strait stays closed until they are met.
There was no sign of a new large-scale US operation on Sunday, and no new strikes were reported. Saturday's mystery explosions on Qeshm Island and along Iran's southern coast remain unattributed: Iranian state television suggested they were related to Iranian military activity in the waterway rather than US strikes, and neither side has confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory. Both sides did keep hitting shipping over the weekend — Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines on an "unauthorised route" and a third tanker exploded, while the US said its air force disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman. Reuters could not confirm any of the reported strikes. Qatar, which is mediating, denied on Saturday that talks had collapsed and said "significant progress" had been made.
The two sides are still far apart on sequencing: Washington insists nuclear issues must feature in the first talks, while Tehran says it will not negotiate on its atomic programme until its core conditions are addressed. The next watch point is Monday, November 9 — the new moon, a dark night favourable for military operations — and the US carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt is not expected in the region before mid-November.
For the world economy, the shipping war is the part that bites: UK maritime monitors said at least 11 ships were attacked in and around the strait over the preceding week, with three sinking, and flows through Hormuz are running at under 60% of capacity. Brent settled around $98 on Friday after a roughly 12% weekly drop.
In short: Trump publicly took a major new Iran campaign off the table — for now, and conditional on a deal — while naming 38 bridges the US could hit if talks fail; Iran is pushing its two-day reopening proposal, Qatar says mediation is alive, and Monday's new moon is the next moment to watch.
Sources:
Source: aapnews.imgdeliver.net.

item.title: Arab states condemn Riyadh attacks; Saudi schools reopen
item.description:
Syria condemned the Houthi attacks on Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District and an Aramco facility on Sunday, pledging "full support for Saudi Arabia" — four days after Syria and Saudi Arabia signed a bilateral defence pact.
Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Egypt issued parallel condemnations. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in Saada used in the Sunday attack on Riyadh, and Saudi schools returned to in-person classes on Sunday after weeks of remote learning because of the airstrikes.
The Houthis said the coalition carried out 105 airstrikes in the last 24 hours, concentrated around Sanaa — that figure is single-source and unverified. (Byte EU · SRN News · Demócrata)
Source: byteseu.com.

item.title: Prosecutors preparing murder charges; suspect still critical
item.description:
Prosecutors are preparing six murder charges against Michał O., 24, over the six people killed in Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday, with the figure able to rise to nine if the deaths of his parents and sister at the family home are added.
The suspect underwent several operations overnight and remains in critical condition, so he has not yet been formally detained or questioned because of his medical condition. Prosecutors formally opened a terrorism investigation on Sunday.
Poland is in national mourning today and Monday; the next test comes Wednesday, Independence Day, when the annual march traditionally brings the radical right onto the streets. (EuropeSays · Le Monde)
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Nvidia GTC keynote tomorrow; Apple trims engineers' AI budgets
item.description:
Nvidia's global virtual GTC conference runs November 8–11, with CEO Jensen Huang's keynote livestreamed Monday, November 9 at 9 a.m.
CET — the next big Nvidia moment after the RTX Spark launch. Separately, Bloomberg reported that Apple cut its engineers' daily AI spending limit from $300 to $200 last month, with some teams possibly dropping to $100 — a small but telling sign of how expensive frontier-model usage has become even inside Apple.
And Reuters reported Nvidia is financing billions of dollars in factories and equipment at Taiwan's Siliconware Precision Industries to ease an AI-chip packaging bottleneck. (Nvidia Newsroom · NoloWiz · TradingView/Benzinga)
Source: nvidianews.nvidia.com.

item.title: sherlock still leads; new: a Wi-Fi accelerator and a fleet of coding agents
item.description:
GitHub's daily trending barely moved: sherlock-project/sherlock is still #1, gaining about 2,400 stars a day, with morluto/rea (~442k stars) and storytold/craft-anything (~22k) holding the top spots.
New names to know: Th0rgal/satmux, a tool that speeds up high-latency GEO in-flight Wi-Fi with warm BBR TCP multiplexing; stablyai/orca, which runs a fleet of coding agents (Claude Code, Codex and others) from your own subscription across desktop, mobile and remote runtimes, at about 119k stars; and google/elephant-goldfish-model, an open-source plugin for designing and reviewing software with agents. AMD also open-sourced PrimusClaw, the managed agent runtime behind its own Instinct GPU clusters, which it says has run in production since April.
(GhTrends · Trendar · FindaRepo · Another Daily AI Newsletter)
Source: ghtrends.dev.

item.title: Norway's aid agency breached — all 20,614 portal users exposed
item.description:
Norway's Agency for Development Cooperation (Norad) disclosed that attackers may have accessed the names and email addresses of all 20,614 registered users of its Grants Portal, which serves 12,511 aid organisations worldwide.
The attackers got in on October 30 by abusing 27 compromised user accounts, and also stole grant-application information from at least three organisations. Norad says it cannot rule out that the attackers saw the names of applicants operating in conflict zones and authoritarian states — the most serious part of this breach.
The portal was shut down immediately; Norway's Data Protection Authority, National Security Authority and police have been notified. Why it matters: this is a registry of aid workers, some in dangerous places, and the attacker is still unknown.
(Norad · The Register)
Source: norad.no.

item.title: Microsoft Paint has an unauthenticated RCE — update via the Store, not Windows Update
item.description:
A newly disclosed unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Windows Paint (CVE-2026-83844) is fixed via a Microsoft Store update, not a standard Windows Update — so it is easy to miss. (PwnSpectrum)
KEV status: no new CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities additions on Sunday. The catalog stands at 1,769 entries; the SonicWall SSLVPN flaw (CVE-2026-19868) federal deadline is November 20. Japan approved a ¥10 billion (about $63 million) emergency cybersecurity package this week. (TheCyberMind weekly brief)
Source: feed.anmolsinghyadav.com.

item.title: Eisenkot formally gets the mandate; Ra'am will back him
item.description:
Gadi Eisenkot formally received the mandate to form Israel's next government from President Isaac Herzog at a ceremony at the President's Residence on Sunday at 5 p.m. He has 28 days, plus a possible 14-day extension, to build a coalition needing 61 seats. Haaretz reported that the Arab party Ra'am will support an Eisenkot-led government, while the Joint List will not vote for it but will not seek to topple it — likely abstaining. The Knesset is sworn in on Tuesday, November 10. (New Kerala · Indian Economic Observer)
No fresh developments: Russell Brand's sentencing is Monday, November 9; FTC v. Amazon, the Netanyahu trial and the Murdaugh retrial (next hearing November 13) are all quiet.
Source: newkerala.com.

item.title: Russia hits Ukraine's grid for a second straight night as talks near
item.description:
Russia kept hammering Ukraine's energy system overnight into Sunday, launching three guided missiles and 164 drones — 112 of them jet-powered — at targets across the country. Ukraine's air force said it shot down or suppressed 137 of the drones by 8 a.m., with hits recorded at 23 locations and debris falling at six more.
The damage is piling up on top of Saturday's much heavier barrage of 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones. DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, said the overnight attack left more than 600,000 people without power in the eastern Dnipropetrovsk region, including the districts of Pavlohrad, Samar and Kamianske and the city of Dnipro itself. The company said the strikes damaged one of its facilities in the Kyiv region and substations run by the national grid operator Ukrenergo — the substations that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv, the surrounding region and central Ukraine. Emergency power cuts are in place in Kyiv, Kharkiv, Sumy and Poltava, with scheduled outages across most other regions. A 75-year-old man injured in a drone strike on Brovary, near Kyiv, died in hospital overnight.
Russia's defence ministry said on Sunday its forces had also hit a power substation in the Zhytomyr region and a container ship south-west of Odesa, claiming both supported Ukrainian military operations. A Russian regional governor said one person was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Kursk region, after a drone hit a tractor in the village of Pervomayskoe.
Zelenskyy said in his nightly address that only four of Saturday's 36 ballistic missiles were intercepted, and blamed a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors. Six ballistic missiles were fired at Kyiv's Northern Bridge, he said, and four struck it; the bridge is closed for repairs. Over the past week, he said, Russia launched 115 missiles, nearly 1,900 guided bombs and more than 3,000 attack drones at Ukrainian cities. He added that some of Saturday's missiles were North Korean-made KN-23s.
Kyiv's argument is that it cannot stop the ballistic campaign without more interceptors, and that Washington is best placed to help — the US approved a $2.1 billion Patriot sale last month, but those missiles are not yet manufactured and are not expected to arrive until well into the 2030s, so Kyiv is pressing the Pentagon to hand over missiles from its own stocks now. Moscow's line is that it is striking military-industrial, energy and transport targets, not civilians. Washington, meanwhile, is still talking up a deal: Trump met Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House on Thursday and said a "big agreement" was coming, and negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the United States are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, November 10–11.
For ordinary Ukrainians the timing is the worst part. Temperatures in Kyiv are near freezing, and the strikes are landing on heating, water and power just as winter sets in. Kyiv's water supply was only just restored after its worst outage of the war, and repair crews are now working around the clock while the grid is hit again night after night.
In short: Russia's energy campaign is escalating into a second consecutive night of heavy strikes, with more than 600,000 people cut off in one region alone and Kyiv's defences running short of the interceptors that stop ballistic missiles — three days before the next round of talks in Abu Dhabi.
Sources:
Source: anewz.tv.

item.title: Mystery blasts on Qeshm Island as both sides report ships hit in the Gulf
item.description:
Explosions were heard on Saturday evening on Qeshm Island and in Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas in southern Iran, and nobody has clearly said what caused them. Iranian state media reported the blasts, and the semi-official Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm, with no official information on possible damage. Iranian state television, though, suggested the explosions might be related to Iranian military activity in the waterway rather than US strikes, and said officials had not confirmed any missile strikes on Iranian territory. Neither Iran nor the United States has commented on the Tasnim report.
The blasts came a day after President Trump confirmed a limited US strike on Friday on an Iranian air-defence system on Qeshm, which he called "minor" and said took about 15 minutes. Washington said on November 2 that it had struck the island in a limited defensive measure after Iranians used surface-to-air missiles against US assets.
Both sides also reported hitting ships over the weekend. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said two oil tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while trying to pass through an "unauthorized route" in the Strait of Hormuz, and the semi-official Fars news agency later reported a third tanker had suffered an explosion and caught fire. The US military said on Saturday evening that its air force had fired at the stern of a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman, disabling it as it tried to get through the blockade. UK monitors reported a separate incident involving a bulk carrier and military forces about 18 nautical miles east of Khor Fakkan in the UAE, with damage unknown. Reuters said it was not able to confirm any of the reported strikes.
Tehran's position, repeated by its officials this week, is that the strait stays closed until Washington meets all seven of its conditions — sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations among them — while Washington insists nuclear issues must feature in the first talks. Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday, saying the US was reviewing it. Qatar, which is mediating, denied reports on Saturday that the US and Iran had failed to reach a deal; its prime minister said both sides were continuing to work toward an agreement and that "significant progress" had been made. On Saturday the US military also announced a new task force to crack down on weapons and sanctioned material reaching Iran by land and across the Caspian Sea; the Revolutionary Guards dismissed it as "wordplay".
For the world economy the shipping war is the part that bites. UK maritime monitors said at least 11 ships had been attacked in and around the strait over the preceding week, with three sinking. Brent crude settled around $98 on Friday after a roughly 12% weekly drop, and flows through the strait are running at under 60% of capacity, with US diesel reserves below 100 million barrels for the first time in more than 20 years.
In short: a day after the US confirmed a strike on Qeshm, new explosions there have no clear cause and no one claiming them, both sides say they hit ships in the Gulf, and Qatar insists mediation is still alive — with Monday's new moon, a dark night favourable for military operations, now the next watch point.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Houthis hit Riyadh again; Aramco building damaged, Yemen toll rises to 33
item.description:
Houthi forces claimed six missile and drone operations against Saudi Arabia on Saturday, saying they targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Aramco oil facilities in Riyadh and Khurais, a National Guard camp in Najran, and military positions in Marib and al-Jawf. The group said the attacks were retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen. Saudi Arabia did not confirm the Houthi claims of successful hits.
What Saudi Arabia did confirm is damage in its own capital. The energy ministry said on Sunday that falling debris caused limited damage to an administrative building belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District, with no injuries or fatalities. A Reuters witness reported shattered windows across several floors of the Aramco Tower. Coalition spokesman Major General Turki al-Malki said air defences intercepted two ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh, along with two cruise missiles targeting the capital and the southern region, plus a ballistic missile heading toward the Eastern Province and a drone targeting the south.
Meanwhile the death toll from Saturday's strikes on al-Shariyah village, east of Sanaa, has risen to 33 killed — including 13 children and eight women — and 39 wounded, according to the Houthi-run health ministry, which called the toll near-final. The Houthis blame Saudi airstrikes that they say hit homes and rescue teams; Saudi Arabia's Center for International Communication said it was investigating the report and had no immediate public response. Reuters could not independently verify the account. It is one of the deadliest reported attacks since fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned group resumed in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered truce.
The blame game is just as unresolved over Friday's attack on al-Hadara market in Taiz, which Houthi health officials say killed 30 people and wounded eight. The Houthis accuse Saudi aircraft of three airstrikes on the crowded market; the Yemeni government and local Taiz authorities say a Houthi ballistic missile hit the market and deny any airstrikes took place in the district that day. Neither account has been independently verified. Sources told South24 that more than ten coalition airstrikes hit Houthi positions along the Taiz–Lahj fronts on Saturday night.
The Houthis say they are hitting Saudi airports, oil facilities and military sites until the airstrikes and blockade end, and they have again warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace. Riyadh says its defences are intercepting the attacks and that it is striking Houthi launchers and infrastructure in Yemen. The UN says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since major fighting resumed.
In short: the Houthis struck at Riyadh and Aramco facilities again on Saturday, debris damaged an Aramco building in the capital, and the reported civilian toll in Yemen climbed to 33 in one village — with both sides still blaming each other for the market attack in Taiz and no independent verification of either claim.
Sources:
Source: anewz.tv.

item.title: Krakow: the three bodies at the gunman's home were his parents and sister
item.description:
Polish police confirmed on Sunday morning that the three people found dead at the Krakow gunman's family home are his parents and his sister. The bodies — a 53-year-old father, a 52-year-old mother and a 20-year-old sister, all with apparent gunshot wounds — were found on Saturday evening at the family apartment in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometres north-east of Krakow. Police have not confirmed whether the suspect killed them before travelling to Krakow, and post-mortems are under way to establish how and when they died.
The suspect has been named by prosecutors as Michał O., a 24-year-old Polish national from Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski with no criminal record and no previous contact with law enforcement. On Saturday at about 3 p.m. he drove into Krakow's Main Market Square and opened fire with an AR-15 rifle from his car, killing six people — four women and two men, including a British citizen — and wounding 15 others. Police confronted him within about three minutes of the first report and arrested him a few streets away after a shootout lasting around 20 minutes; two officers were wounded, one critically. The suspect was seriously wounded in the exchange of gunfire, underwent several operations overnight and remains in critical condition, so prosecutors have not yet been able to question him or formally present charges. Police recovered seven firearms from the family apartment and are investigating their ownership; Polish media report the weapons belonged to his father, who was registered at a sport shooting club.
Prosecutors announced on Sunday that they are investigating the shooting as an act of a "terrorist nature", working with the Internal Security Agency. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said preliminary findings pointed to a young man "fascinated by far-right ideologies" with radical ultranationalist views, and the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime has joined the investigation to examine possible links to radical groups online. No motive has been established, and no accomplices or organisational links have been confirmed. Disinformation spread quickly overnight: social media accounts tried to link the gunman to Ukraine, the United States or the Polish left, claims the authorities and the press have refuted. The defence ministry confirmed he was not a soldier, despite the military-style clothing he wore.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who travelled to Krakow on Saturday evening, called it terrorism and said: "Until now, Poland had never experienced a terrorist incident this serious." Former president Bronisław Komorowski called it the first time in Poland that an attack had been carried out with a long automatic weapon with such dramatic consequences. The shooting follows a rise in violence in Poland — three attacks on schools between late September and early October, and an October 11 plot against Tusk and his defence minister that police foiled — and it lands in the middle of a bitter political standoff over the Constitutional Tribunal, with the nationalist right accusing the government of repression and the government accusing its critics of exploiting the tragedy. Tusk appealed to political leaders "not to use this tragedy for your own ends."
Poland is in national mourning on Sunday and Monday, with Krakow's mourning running through November 11. The first test of whether the calls for unity hold comes on Wednesday, Poland's national holiday, when the annual independence march traditionally brings the radical right onto the streets.
In short: the Krakow attack is now a nine-dead case — six people shot in the square and the gunman's parents and sister found dead at home — with the suspect in critical condition, no motive established, and prosecutors treating it as a suspected terrorist offence as Poland begins two days of national mourning.
Sources:
Source: anewz.tv.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said preliminary findings pointed to a young man "fascinated by far-right ideologies" with radical ultranationalist views, and the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime has joined the investigation to examine possible links to radical groups online. No motive has been established, and no accomplices or organisational links have been confirmed. Disinformation spread quickly overnight: social media accounts tried to link the gunman to Ukraine, the United States or the Polish left, claims the authorities and the press have refuted. The defence ministry confirmed he was not a soldier, despite the military-style clothing he wore.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who travelled to Krakow on Saturday evening, called it terrorism and said: "Until now, Poland had never experienced a terrorist incident this serious." Former president Bronisław Komorowski called it the first time in Poland that an attack had been carried out with a long automatic weapon with such dramatic consequences. The shooting follows a rise in violence in Poland — three attacks on schools between late September and early October, and an October 11 plot against Tusk and his defence minister that police foiled — and it lands in the middle of a bitter political standoff over the Constitutional Tribunal, with the nationalist right accusing the government of repression and the government accusing its critics of exploiting the tragedy. Tusk appealed to political leaders "not to use this tragedy for your own ends."

Poland is in national mourning on Sunday and Monday, with Krakow's mourning running through November 11. The first test of whether the calls for unity hold comes on Wednesday, Poland's national holiday, when the annual independence march traditionally brings the radical right onto the streets.

In short: the Krakow attack is now a nine-dead case — six people shot in the square and the gunman's parents and sister found dead at home — with the suspect in critical condition, no motive established, and prosecutors treating it as a suspected terrorist offence as Poland begins two days of national mourning.

item.title: GPT-6 Cyber: OpenAI's Frontier of "Aligned" Security Agents
item.description:
OpenAI launched GPT-6 Cyber on November 5, a version of its GPT-6 Astra model trained specifically for security research: finding flaws, building working exploits and writing patches, all inside authorised scope.
It scores 48.5% on the ExploitGym benchmark, up from 32.1% for its predecessor, and OpenAI says it produced working exploits for 948 Linux privilege-escalation flaws and found 81 previously unknown high-severity bugs in Firefox — Mozilla has already shipped fixes for many of them. The model is rated "Critical" for cyber capability under OpenAI's own framework, and it is gated to vetted researchers in the Daybreak Red programme, not available to ordinary users.
Why it matters: this is the model behind the Brotli RCE (CVE-2026-111497) finding, and it shows AI-written exploit research is now operating at industrial scale — defenders get the bugs found faster, but the same capability in the wrong hands is the threat. (Cyber Magazine)
Source: cybermagazine.com.

item.title: Fake GitHub tools backdoor security teams
item.description:
A campaign pushing fake security utilities on GitHub has compromised more than 2,000 Windows systems with backdoors and information stealers, according to Cyware's November 7 threat briefing. The malicious packages were published as version 1.0.1 on November 1, flagged as malware 70 seconds later and removed by 09:13 UTC — but the window was enough. Why it matters: the people being targeted are security professionals themselves, and the lesson is the same one as the LiteLLM and OVHcloud hijacks — verify what you install, even when it looks like a security tool. (Cyware)
KEV status: no new CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities additions since the SonicWall SSLVPN flaw (CVE-2026-19868) on November 6, federal deadline November 20. The WordPress core flaw (CVE-2026-119977) federal deadline passed on November 6. (TheCyberMind weekly brief)
Source: cyware.com.

item.title: Iran: new explosions along the Strait of Hormuz coast — and Washington is squeezing Tehran on land as well as at sea
item.description:
Fresh explosions were reported on Saturday evening along Iran's southern coast — on Qeshm Island and in the port cities of Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas — with no official explanation of what caused them and no confirmation from the United States that it was responsible. The blasts came a day after President Trump confirmed new US strikes on Iranian air defences on Qeshm, and on the same day Washington announced a new task force aimed at choking off Iran's overland supply routes. Qatar's mediation continues in parallel, with signs Tehran may be willing to discuss parts of its nuclear programme it had previously ruled out.
The details of Saturday's blasts are thin and conflicting. Iranian state television reported explosion-like sounds on Qeshm Island and in Sirik, Jask and Bandar Abbas, all close to the Strait of Hormuz; the state news agency IRNA reported two explosions in the eastern part of Qeshm, and residents reported hearing explosions in Jask. Earlier on Saturday, the semi-official Tasnim news agency said two missiles had struck Qeshm, without saying who fired them. A state television reporter suggested the sounds could be related to Iranian military operations to defend the strait, though no official confirmation has established that. Israel's N12 reported that people in Iran were speaking of casualties at the port of Jask, without giving a number, and that a senior Iranian official had threatened retaliation against American interests — again without naming the official or saying who Iran holds responsible. No US statement about Saturday's blasts has appeared, and no damage or casualty figures have been released.
What is confirmed is the previous round. Trump told reporters on Friday night, en route to Mar-a-Lago, that US forces had carried out "minor strikes" on an Iranian air-defence system on Qeshm Island: "They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five." Iranian media reported two missiles hitting the Suza area of Qeshm, and Iran claimed it shot down an American MQ-9 drone — and separately an MQ-1 — claims the US has not confirmed. US Central Command described the situation on the island as "relatively calm." It was the first US strike since Tuesday's midterm elections, and the second round on Qeshm this week after limited defensive strikes on Monday, November 2. On Saturday, CENTCOM announced a new 20-strong Task Force Iron Gate, under Adm. Brad Cooper, to stop Iran using ground routes to move advanced weapons and dual-use materials, coordinating with unnamed US government agencies across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea. CENTCOM said the naval blockade had bottled up $25 billion in Iranian crude oil.
The two sides are describing the same moment in opposite terms. Trump's argument, made to reporters on Friday night, is that the war was necessary and that Iran is now eager to deal: "We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said, adding that "if we didn't hit Iran, you wouldn't have Israel today." His administration is split on what comes next — Axios reported earlier that Vice President Vance and envoy Steve Witkoff favour a deal, Defence Secretary Hegseth and Israel's Netanyahu favour renewed major combat, and Treasury Secretary Bessent and CIA Director Ratcliffe favour keeping the blockade and pressure without war or a deal. Tehran's position, repeated by its officials, is that it will not negotiate on its nuclear programme or reopen the strait until the US meets its seven conditions, including ending the blockade, lifting sanctions, unfreezing assets and paying war compensation — and its army spokesman warned on Saturday that retaliation against US bases would have "no geographical limitations" if Iran is attacked. But Bloomberg reported on Saturday, citing a diplomat familiar with the talks, that Iran is showing a willingness to discuss aspects of its nuclear programme that had previously been off the table. Under the latest Qatari proposal, the US would lift the blockade and release some frozen Iranian assets while Iran would allow IAEA inspectors back into its bombed nuclear sites. Qatar's prime minister said Saturday that mediation remained active and Washington was still willing to find a solution; Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he had spoken with 12 foreign ministers in 48 hours.
For ordinary people, the stakes are measured in fuel and shipping. At least 11 ships were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the past week, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations, and three of them sank. Oil settled lower on Friday — Brent at $98.32 — on hopes of a deal, but fresh explosions near the strait could reverse that quickly, and US diesel reserves are already below 100 million barrels for the first time in more than 20 years. There is still no ceasefire in force, the US naval blockade continues, and Monday, November 9 is a new moon — the dark conditions commanders prefer for air operations — which is why it remains the date to watch.
In short: explosions were reported Saturday evening on Qeshm Island and in Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas, with the cause unconfirmed and no US statement — a day after Trump confirmed Friday strikes on Qeshm air defences and CENTCOM announced a new task force to cut Iran's overland supply routes. Qatar's mediation continues, with Bloomberg reporting Iran may now discuss nuclear issues it had ruled out, but Tehran's seven conditions still stand and there is no ceasefire.
Sources:
Source: nypost.com.

item.title: Israel: Herzog picks Eisenkot to try to form a government — but the maths to a majority is brutal
item.description:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced on Saturday evening that he will task Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief who leads the Yashar party, with forming Israel's next government, handing Benjamin Netanyahu a political setback after the October 27 election left parliament without a clear majority. The formal handover of the mandate is scheduled for Sunday at 5 p.m. at the President's Residence in Jerusalem, starting a 28-day clock — extendable by up to 14 days — for Eisenkot to build a coalition.
The decision followed several days of consultations with the parties in the 120-seat Knesset. Factions representing 67 lawmakers recommended Eisenkot, while 46 backed Netanyahu and a faction holding seven seats declined to recommend either. Herzog had said on Thursday, at the end of the formal consultations, that he would keep talking to political figures over the weekend before deciding; those talks included separate meetings with Netanyahu and Eisenkot. But the recommendation tally is not the same as a coalition. In the election, Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc won 53 seats and Eisenkot's four-party alliance won 48 — neither reaches the 61 needed for a majority. Eisenkot's 67 recommendations include 19 from the two Arab-led parties, the Joint List (11) and Ra'am (8), and he has ruled out forming a government with them as formal coalition partners. Avigdor Lieberman, leader of Yisrael Beiteinu in Eisenkot's own alliance, has said he would oppose a government dependent on Arab-led parties. Herzog himself warned that the numbers were not the whole story: "The results of the consultations may appear clear, but the authority vested in me by law is to determine who has the ability to form a government, and that is not entirely clear, given the mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves."
The two camps are pitching very different governments. Eisenkot said on Friday that he intends to form a national emergency government, and his supporters present him as the candidate who can end a long period of political deadlock. Netanyahu's camp argues that the election result — his bloc won more seats than Eisenkot's — means he remains the more natural prime minister, and Netanyahu has seized on a vote-tampering investigation to cast doubt on the process, though the Central Election Committee said the integrity of the vote was not compromised. If Eisenkot cannot form a government within the allotted period, Herzog may nominate another candidate, and if no candidate succeeds, Israel will hold a new election. Netanyahu remains prime minister in a caretaker role while negotiations continue, and the new Knesset is due to be sworn in on Tuesday, November 10.
For Israelis, the practical consequence is weeks of coalition bargaining before any new government can take office — and possibly another election if the maths does not work. A caretaker government cannot take major decisions, and the deadlock comes while Israel is still managing the aftermath of the war in Gaza and the wider regional confrontation with Iran. Eisenkot's initial mandate expires on December 6, with a possible extension to December 20.
In short: President Herzog has chosen Gadi Eisenkot to try first to form Israel's next government, with the formal mandate handed over on Sunday and 28 days to build a coalition. Eisenkot has 67 recommendations to Netanyahu's 46, but his bloc holds only 48 seats and needs 61 — and the 19 Arab-party recommendations that got him the mandate come from parties he has ruled out as coalition partners, so the path to a majority is far from clear.
Sources:
Source: themedialine.org.

item.title: The death toll from the Russian bombing of the humanitarian aid point at Komyshuvakha has risen to 55
item.description:
, according to a war briefing summarising Saturday's reporting — up from 53 on Friday.
The aid point was hit by a 3-ton glide bomb earlier in the week, with a second strike hitting a shelter. Separately, Ukraine struck the Proton plant in Oryol, which makes components for the Iskander ballistic missiles fired at Kyiv hours earlier, and Russian media reported a Ukrainian hit on the Saratov refinery (unconfirmed).
Chernihiv was reported fully blacked out after Friday night's barrage, and DTEK imposed emergency outages across Kyiv region. A Naftogaz oil and gas facility in central Ukraine was struck three times, sparking a large fire.
Source: youtube.com.

item.description:
, about 120 miles north of Krakow. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said there are "strong indications" they are members of the suspect's immediate family.
The suspect, a 24-year-old Polish citizen, underwent multiple surgeries and is in a "stable but very critical condition," a regional police spokesperson told Reuters. Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz denied reports the man was a soldier: "The man was not and is not a soldier in the Polish Armed Forces and has never had anything to do with the military."

item.description:
in Saturday's airstrikes on al-Shariya village, east of Sanaa — up from the 25 killed reported in the evening brief.
The ministry said the strikes hit homes in the Bani Hushaysh district and that most of those killed were women and children; a hospital director said many victims remained trapped under the rubble, including first responders. The ministry's figures changed several times during the day (11, then 22, then 25, then 27 dead), so treat the toll as still fluid.

item.title: Ukraine: only 4 of 36 Russian ballistic missiles were intercepted — and Kyiv says North Korean missiles hit a key power plant
item.description:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Ukraine's air defences shot down only four of the 36 ballistic missiles Russia fired at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight — and that preliminary examinations at the impact sites indicate Russia used North Korean-made KN-23 missiles to hit one of the key energy facilities damaged in the attack. It is the sharpest public admission yet of how thin Ukraine's missile shield has become, days before trilateral talks open in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday.
The details Zelenskyy gave after a coordination call on the damage paint a stark picture. Ukraine's energy facilities were hit 18 times in the past 24 hours, according to First Deputy Prime Minister and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal. Zelenskyy said there is still "a significant shortage of interceptors for Patriot systems, and the United States is in the best position to help address it," and that Kyiv is working "at every level" to speed up deliveries. He also ordered the interior minister and Kyiv's city administration to prepare backup public transport routes and extra transport for the capital — noting that, at present, such contingency plans are "practically nonexistent" at the municipal level. G7-format meetings are being prepared, Zelenskyy said, with new European contributions expected to the PURL initiative that funds US weapons purchases for Ukraine, plus new energy support packages.
The two sides describe the same night in opposite terms. Zelenskyy's argument is that the escalation is deliberate pressure ahead of the talks: "By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine's position and that of its partners," he said, adding that "Russia has a very particular view of diplomacy — as a subtype of aggression." He also used the KN-23 finding to argue that global sanctions "need to be significantly strengthened — against everyone in the world who provides their 'services' in destroying lives." Moscow's defence ministry, as reported in the morning brief, said it struck military-industrial, energy and transport targets, claiming it hit Kyiv's Northern Bridge because it was being used to move weapons and a plant it says produces Flamingo cruise missiles. Russia has not responded to the KN-23 claim, and the missile identification is preliminary — examinations at the sites are ongoing.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the interception rate is the number that matters. Kyiv's power, heating and water situation was already described by the mayor as "extremely difficult" after the overnight barrage, with temperatures near freezing. If only one in nine ballistic missiles can be stopped, every new salvo lands harder — and the Patriot shortage is now the bottleneck Zelenskyy is pressing Washington on, openly, in the days before negotiators sit down. The talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10–11 go ahead as planned; nothing in Saturday's reporting suggests the date has changed.
In short: of the 36 ballistic missiles Russia fired at Kyiv overnight, Ukraine intercepted only four — and preliminary findings say North Korean KN-23 missiles were used against a key energy facility. Zelenskyy is publicly pressing the US for Patriot interceptors before Tuesday's Abu Dhabi talks, arguing Russia is bombing to gain leverage at the table.
Sources:
Source: europesays.com.

item.title: Poland: gunman kills six in Krakow's Main Market Square — police say far-right influence is being investigated
item.description:
A gunman drove into Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon and opened fire at random from his car, killing six people and wounding 15, before police shot and detained him. It is the worst mass shooting in Poland in living memory, in a country that has long seen itself as safer from such attacks than its western European neighbours. The shooting happened at around 3 p.m. local time — just as this morning's brief was being published — so this is the first brief carrying it.
The facts as Polish authorities have confirmed them: the attacker was a 24-year-old Polish citizen who drove into the historic square — packed with tourists and locals on a Saturday afternoon — and fired at people from his vehicle. Police said he wore military-style clothes, used an AR-15 rifle he held a firearms licence for, and had "many weapons and ammunition" in his vehicle. Officers fired at him three minutes after the first report came in, according to Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski, who praised them for preventing "a much larger massacre." Two police officers were wounded in the shootout, one of them shot three times and in critical condition. The six dead were four women and two men; one of the dead was a British citizen, and five of the injured were foreign nationals, including a Portuguese woman. Krakow's mayor declared city mourning through November 11, and President Karol Nawrocki said he would declare national mourning on November 8 and 9.
What is still unclear is why he did it. Kierwinski told a news briefing that "everything points to the fact that the shooter was influenced by far-right ideology, a matter that will also be subject to investigation" — but police have not named a motive, and the ideology angle is an early indication, not an established finding. The shooting also follows a string of school stabbings in Poland in October that authorities linked to violent extremist content online, which Reuters noted as part of the unease in the country. Polish media reported that three members of the gunman's family were found dead at his home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski earlier in the day; police have not confirmed that, though Reuters reported Internal Security Agency agents were sent to the family home as well as the scene.
The political reaction was immediate and, unusually, restrained. Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who travelled to Krakow after meeting the security services, called the shooting terrorism and appealed to politicians "of all stripes" not to exploit the tragedy, saying "we will establish all the circumstances of this crime." President Zelenskyy called it "shocking" and offered condolences, and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said it was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland." The suspect is in hospital in serious condition after being shot by police; the only known perpetrator is in custody, and police say there is no continuing threat to the public.
In short: six people were killed and 15 wounded when a gunman opened fire at random in Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon. Police shot and detained the 24-year-old suspect within minutes; the interior minister says early indications point to far-right influence, but the motive is still under investigation. National mourning runs November 8–9.
Sources:
Source: 985theriver.com.

item.title: Tech: AI stocks whipsawed after the midterms — and a memory crunch is now squeezing Apple, Nvidia and PC prices
item.description:
Wall Street's AI trade had its wildest two days in months. On Thursday, November 5, the Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.52% to 24,315 — its steepest drop since April 2025 — with the S&P 500 down 4.36% and the Dow down 3.44%. Nvidia fell 9.26%, AMD 17.26%, Micron 17.46% and SanDisk 22.26%. The trigger, according to market reporting, was post-midterm anxiety: with Democrats taking control of the House and Senate, investors feared tighter oversight of AI data centers and federal AI spending. On Friday the market bounced back part of the way — the Nasdaq rose 1.09% to 24,579.42, with AMD up 11.04%, Micron 5.12% and Nvidia 2.78% — but the index still lost 3.4% on the week, its fourth straight weekly decline, and the S&P 500 lost 2.7%.
Underneath the whipsaw sits a slower, more structural squeeze: memory. AI servers built around Nvidia and AMD accelerators need huge amounts of high-bandwidth memory, DRAM and fast storage, and memory makers have been steering wafers toward those customers. TrendForce forecasts conventional DRAM contract prices up another 10%–15% this quarter and NAND flash up 15%–20%, with DRAM supply staying tight into 2027. The sellers are making extraordinary money — Micron reported an 81% operating margin on $54.23 billion of quarterly revenue (up 379% year on year), SanDisk 80% and SK hynix 80% — while Samsung said its 2027 HBM supply is already sold out and SK hynix said supply will fall short of demand through 2030.
Apple is the clearest case of a buyer paying up. Its fiscal 2026 annual report says it is experiencing "supply constraints and rising costs driven by industry-wide supply-demand imbalances" and expects them to intensify for memory and storage. Apple guided its December-quarter gross margin to 45%–46%, citing memory costs first and the cost of its Siri AI ramp second, and its manufacturing purchase obligations rose by $33 billion in a single quarter, to $89.7 billion. Lower-margin products have less room to absorb it: PC makers are shipping smaller SSDs to hold prices down, and AMD's gaming revenue fell 40% in the third quarter. Nvidia, meanwhile, is moving deeper into the memory stack itself — asking Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to build the base dies of its custom NVHBM on TSMC's 3nm process — and TSMC confirmed it has begun planning 3D DRAM at Nvidia's request, though it says it will stay a logic foundry.
For ordinary buyers, this is the part that lands in the wallet: the same AI boom that lifted chip stocks is making the memory inside phones, laptops and consoles more expensive, and the crunch is expected to last into 2027. Apple's approach so far has been to absorb the cost rather than raise prices, but its margin guidance shows the pressure is real.
In short: AI stocks crashed 5.5% on Thursday on post-midterm regulation fears, then bounced 1.1% on Friday — but the Nasdaq still ended the week down 3.4%. Behind the swings, a memory shortage is pushing DRAM and NAND prices up another 10%–20% this quarter, memory makers are earning ~80% margins, and Apple is guiding its own margins down because of memory costs.
Sources:
Source: mitrade.com.

item.title: Houthi media reported at least 25 people killed, including women and children, in a Saudi airstrike on al-Shariyah, a town east of the Yemeni capital Sanaa, on Saturday
item.description:
Al Masirah television, run by the Houthis, broadcast footage of rescuers pulling bodies from rubble, and the Houthi-run Saba news agency said Saudi Arabia carried out the attack.
The Saudi-led coalition had not commented at the time of reporting, and the claim is single-source — it has not been independently confirmed. Hours before the strike, the coalition said it had intercepted a missile heading toward Riyadh, and Houthi leader Mahdi al-Mashat vowed the group would take revenge for the latest attacks.
The UN says more than 1,600 people have been killed and over 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in Yemen. This follows Friday's disputed market attack in Taiz, covered in the morning brief, where at least 30 were killed and each side blames the other.
Source: securitysignal.com.

item.title: Chainalysis breach widened sharply — catch-up, first reported here
item.description:
The blockchain analytics firm, whose software is used by the FBI, IRS Criminal Investigation and banks, said on November 4 that names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for *all* of its users had been exposed to a malicious actor, and that some KYT transaction-screening accounts appear to have been accessed without authorization.
The company first disclosed the incident on October 30, describing an attacker using "offensive agentic techniques." It took KYT, Reactor, its login page and other products offline, and began restoring KYT and Address Screening on November 6 behind IP allowlisting, with mandatory password resets and API key rotation.
Chainalysis says it has no evidence investigations data was accessed or its attribution data manipulated, but the investigation is still open.
Source: ccn.com.

item.description:
CVE-2024-27834, an improper-authentication flaw in multiple Apple products (CVSS 5.5), is now listed as actively exploited, with a federal patch deadline of November 18.
It was fixed long ago — Safari 17.5, iOS/iPadOS 17.5 and 16.7.8 — so the action is to make sure old devices are actually updated. The SonicWall SSL-VPN flaw CVE-2026-19868, added Friday, was covered in the morning brief.

NVIDIA/auto-ontology (9.5k) is a Python framework for building semantic, graph-based reasoning layers over data for LLM workflows. ranxianglei/billion-context (4,396 stars) is a context-compression plugin aimed at month-long single sessions. dsx-ai-factory/nvke (338 stars) is NVIDIA's Kubernetes Engine — a management plane for GPU Kubernetes on bare metal. The week's chart is still led by thedotmack/claude-mem (114,380 stars, +8.7k this week) for persistent agent memory, with morluto/rea and storytold/craft-anything still top of the daily board.

item.title: Russell Brand:
item.description:
held at HMP Wandsworth ahead of sentencing on Monday, November 9, after Thursday's conviction on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
His barrister, Ian Winter KC, referred himself to the Bar Standards Board on Friday after confronting Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin outside court minutes after the verdicts; the paper's editor has said Winter should be called to account. The Metropolitan Police confirmed Friday it is investigating two further alleged rapes and expects more women may come forward.
Sentencing expectations run 6–9 years; the judge warned of a "significant" custodial term. Emergency services were called to Wandsworth on Saturday; the nature of the incident is unknown and it was not a fire.
Source: aroundprague.cz.
