item.title: Israel: Eisenkot wins the recommendations, Herzog names his pick on Sunday
item.description:
President Isaac Herzog finished consultations with every Knesset faction on Thursday evening and said he intends to assign the mandate to form a government this coming Sunday, November 8. Factions representing 67 lawmakers recommended Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot; factions representing 46 recommended Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; and United Torah Judaism, with seven seats, declined to recommend anyone. The Joint List, with 11 seats, announced Thursday it would recommend Eisenkot, joining Ra'am's eight — though both Arab-led lists' endorsements don't commit them to joining his coalition, and Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out governing with them.
The arithmetic is the trap. Eisenkot's 67 recommendations are not 67 votes for a government: his core bloc of four Jewish-led parties won only 48 seats, the Arab-led lists won 19, and a majority needs 61 of 120. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in the October 27 election, with Likud the largest single party at 27. Herzog said he still needs to clarify directly with some party leaders who can actually assemble a governing majority, which is why he is taking until Sunday rather than announcing immediately — he has until November 11. The new Knesset is sworn in on November 10, and whoever gets the mandate has 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote — a charge his critics say is an attempt to undermine results he denies trying to undermine. Israel's Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election's integrity had not been compromised, and its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, called on elected officials to protect public trust rather than shake it. "This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power," Sohlberg told Herzog. Netanyahu's far-right allies, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.
For ordinary Israelis, the stakes are a caretaker government running the country while the region stays volatile — Netanyahu remains prime minister until a new coalition is formed, or through another election if no candidate succeeds — and a president openly warning parties to do their utmost to avert another round of voting. Herzog told the factions that "any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility rests upon us."
In short: Eisenkot has the recommendations, 67 to 46, and Herzog will name his pick on Sunday — but recommendations aren't a coalition, and with both men ruling out governing with the Arab parties whose backing put Eisenkot ahead, nobody has shown a path to 61 seats yet. Netanyahu is fighting the result itself, and another election is still on the table.
Sources:
Source: wncy.com.

item.title: Ukraine: aid-centre death toll reaches 42 as Brussels talks turn to security guarantees
item.description:
The death toll from Monday's Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in the village of Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, has risen to 42, police said on Thursday, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year. Up to 33 people remained buried beneath the rubble, with rescue work continuing and bodies still being identified. On Wednesday, regional official Ivan Fedorov had said 59 people were missing. Bodycam footage from one of the police officers killed, which Reuters verified, showed the moments before a second Russian strike hit, destroying the shelter where residents were hiding after a radio warning. Ukraine's national police said the strikes included a 3-ton FAB glide bomb, carrying around 1.4 tons of explosives. Russia's Defence Ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian military units around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements, and that up to 25 Ukrainian servicemen were killed. Both Moscow and Kyiv deny deliberately targeting civilians; the UN human rights mission in Ukraine said on Tuesday that the bombing likely violated international law.
At the same time, the diplomacy track moved to its second day in Brussels. Talks on Ukraine's postwar reconstruction and security guarantees resumed on Thursday at NATO headquarters, with delegations from Ukraine, the US, the UK, France, Germany, the EU and NATO, plus the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock, according to the Associated Press. Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov said the discussions covered postwar reconstruction, funding for 2027 and the security guarantees Western allies could offer, as well as a new post-war European security architecture. US envoy Jared Kushner called the talks "productive and substantive" in a post on X. The Brussels meetings come a week before negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking from an Ibero-American summit in Spain, said in an interview broadcast Thursday that Ukraine must adapt to the new realities of US politics after the Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and that solving the Patriot air-defence issue is the top priority — he is also working to keep enough F-16 fighter jets operating over the next five to six months. He said EU, NATO and US officials meeting in Brussels were making some progress on security-guarantee proposals. Overnight, Russia said it struck logistics and transport targets across Ukraine, including a Nova Poshta logistics hub in Kharkiv region that Moscow said was used to assemble drones, railway locomotives, a power station in Dnipropetrovsk region, and a cargo vessel at sea off Odesa — claims Reuters could not independently verify.
For ordinary Ukrainians, the war's daily shape is unchanged: power generation and substations keep getting hit, emergency outages keep coming, and the people queuing for aid in a frontline village were the ones who paid for Monday's strike. The Brussels talks are about what comes after — a prosperity plan for reconstruction and guarantees meant to stop the next war — but they are being held while the current one is still killing civilians at aid centres.
In short: the Komyshuvakha toll rose to 42 with dozens still buried, the UN says the bombing likely broke international law, and in Brussels the allies spent a second day sketching the post-war guarantees and reconstruction plan — with Zelenskyy now openly recalibrating for a Washington run by Democrats and Patriot missiles at the top of his list.
Sources:
Source: kwsn.com.

item.title: N0n ransomware group published data from Delta Dental of Missouri and The Container Store on Thursday (unverified tracker claims)
item.description:
Delta Dental's leak includes a customer-relationship database with 48,528 email addresses, 17,913 phone numbers, and member records containing names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, home addresses and dental treatment details.
The Container Store leak includes 46,013 customer chat messages, search-session analytics, 9,305 customer email addresses and a staff directory. Both are listed as "not paid — exposed."
The dental insurer leak is the serious one: SSNs plus health details is full identity-theft material.
Source: qpulse.quasarcybertech.com.

item.title: Open source: today's trending
item.description:
GitHub's trending list on Thursday is still dominated by agent tooling, with two notable new entries.
NVIDIA/auto-ontology (+2,707 stars) is a Python framework for building semantic, graph-based reasoning layers over data so AI agents query it with certified metric definitions instead of guessing. cloudflare/security-audit-skill is the strongest debut: installed as a skill, it has your coding agent map a codebase's architecture and trust boundaries, sends isolated hunter agents after the uncovered areas, and hands every candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it before anything reaches the report. Still climbing: storytold/craft-anything (+3,639/day, 14.5k stars), the reverse-engineering explainer; vercel-labs/agent-desktop (+2.5k/day), the computer-use CLI; and garrytan/gstack (139k stars), Garry Tan's exact Claude Code setup with 23 opinionated tools.
Source: trendar.org.

item.title: FTC v. Amazon (ads auction):
item.description:
The FTC and 22 state attorneys general filed an updated complaint on October 28, with the newly unredacted details announced November 5, alleging Amazon secretly raised the prices advertisers paid in its online search advertising auction — by up to 50% above auction results on ordinary days, and up to 250% on major shopping days like Prime Day and Black Friday.
One large food-and-beverage advertiser faced increases of more than 100% during Prime Day 2023, and Amazon internally acknowledged the increases were "destroying campaign performance." Amazon said it strongly disagrees with the claims and that the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate."
The antitrust trial itself is set for March 29, 2027.
Source: searchenginejournal.com.

item.description:
Both sides have now moved for summary judgment — Amazon seeking dismissal, the FTC seeking liability — and at Friday's economics hearing Judge Chun pressed the FTC on what consumer harm it is actually trying to prove, noting "millions of shoppers are happy" with the service.
The jury trial is underway in Seattle. Separately, Amazon agreed to pay $3 million in refunds to eligible Arizona consumers over its old Prime cancellation process, after the state AG sued in 2024; Amazon denied violating Arizona law.

item.title: The secret strikes before the midterms — and the war that paused
item.description:
The United States was quietly bombing Iran in the weeks before Tuesday's midterm elections, and the White House worked to keep it that way. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that American forces carried out a series of limited, unannounced strikes against Iranian targets — missile launchers and other military equipment — in the run-up to November 3, with senior officials discussing the political cost of admitting the attacks were still going on. One operation took place on November 2, the day before Americans voted: US forces struck targets on Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz, after Iranian forces fired a surface-to-air missile at an American fighter jet, according to US officials. The Journal says the strikes were designed to limit Iran's military capability while avoiding casualties, and that Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were part of the discussions, which President Trump approved.
The secrecy is the story. On November 2, the same day as the Qeshm strike, Trump told reporters American forces had "not been engaged in combat for months." The Journal reports administration officials worried that renewed attention to the Iran fighting would damage Republican prospects in the elections — and the elections went badly for them anyway. Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, and Vance has publicly denounced the war as the primary cause of the Republican defeats. Trump has since acknowledged the war contributed to the losses, particularly through gasoline prices, while defending his decision to launch it.
What happens next is genuinely undecided, and the two sides of the administration are pulling in opposite directions. Trump said Wednesday he has no immediate plans for new large-scale strikes, telling the Financial Times "we're locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it," and describing the situation as "a brilliant situation." But Axios reports the US military is finishing preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations, sending more assets to the region, with no final decision made and even Trump's closest aides unsure what he will do. Qatari mediators, meanwhile, are working on a draft agreement that could head off a return to fighting and lead to direct talks in the coming days. Iran's position hasn't moved: its top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, called Washington's reply to Tehran's seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz "not convincing," and the strait stays shut until they are fully met.
For ordinary people, the clearest signal is at the pump. Brent crude fell to $95.07 on Thursday, down almost 10% in a week to its lowest in two months, as the threat of renewed strikes receded. But the damage from months of war is still in the system: EA WorldView reports US diesel reserves have fallen below 100 million barrels for the first time in more than 20 years, and diesel is running about $6.27 a gallon — roughly 75% higher than a year ago, close to an all-time record. Inside Iran, the crackdown continues: Tehran executed two more participants in January's nationwide protests on Wednesday, Amirhossein Maleki and Amirhossein Ebrahimi, sentenced to death over the killing of four police officers in Isfahan.
In short: Washington was fighting a war it wouldn't admit to before the election, the election punished it anyway, and now the choice is between a deal the Qataris are still trying to broker and a new round of strikes the military is already preparing for. Nothing is decided, and the fuel-price pain that helped cost Republicans the midterms hasn't gone away.
Sources:
Source: live.eastoranews.com.

Nothing is decided, and the fuel-price pain that helped cost Republicans the midterms hasn't gone away.

item.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults
item.description:
A jury at Southwark Crown Court in London found Russell Brand guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, after nine hours and thirteen minutes of deliberations spread over three days. The 51-year-old comedian was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand he faced a "significant custodial term," remanded him in custody, and set sentencing for Monday, November 9.
The convictions cover four of the six women who accused Brand of offences between 1999 and 2009. He was found guilty of raping a 21-year-old fan after meeting her at a 2009 stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo; of sexually assaulting a Capital Radio worker in a corridor in 2005; of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker during a forced massage in 2009; and of groping an MTV worker at a Soho bar party in 2004 — though the jury cleared him of orally raping that same woman in a toilet afterwards. He was acquitted of raping a woman after a 1999 Labour Party conference fringe show in Bournemouth, and of trying to drag an MTV worker into a toilet to indecently assault her in 2001.
The trial turned on consent, and the two sides told the jury opposite stories about the same facts. Brand testified that he had "misused" his fame "very, very selfishly" for sexual encounters in the past, but insisted he never engaged in non-consensual activity — "consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and in many ways, more important than sex itself." His barrister, Ian Winter, argued the case was "thoroughly contaminated" by Channel 4's 2023 Dispatches documentary, saying the complainants only came forward at the programme's invitation and the publicity made a fair trial impossible. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones pushed back in closing, noting the six women did not know each other and had nothing to gain: no limelight, no documentary appearance, no compensation claims — only, she said, "perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago."
For the women, the verdict ends a case that began with the 2023 joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4, and ran for three weeks of testimony in which Brand himself took the stand. Brand stood straight and still in the dock as the verdicts were read, closing his eyes when the rape conviction was announced, and told his wife Laura Gallacher "I love you" before being taken into custody. The Metropolitan Police told Sky News they are investigating Brand over other rape allegations made by two more women, so this may not be the last case.
In short: after a three-week trial and three days of deliberations, a jury believed four of the six women and disbelieved two of the most serious allegations — a mixed verdict that still leaves Brand, 51, facing a significant prison sentence on Monday.
Sources:
Source: usatoday.com.

item.title: Ukraine overnight: quieter night, but the refinery war goes on
item.description:
Russia launched 2 missiles and 128 drones at Ukraine overnight, with 105 shot down or neutralized, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
One person was injured in the Kyiv region when a Russian attack set a logistics facility ablaze. Ukraine hit back at the Ryazan oil refinery, where a drone attack set off a large fire — at least six hits recorded — injuring one person, damaging power lines and shattering windows at a school, prompting class cancellations.
Russia's Defence Ministry claimed 496 Ukrainian drones were intercepted. The toll from Monday's strike on the Komyshuvakha aid centre stands at 40 dead.
Today in Brussels, Ukraine, the US, France, Germany, the UK, NATO and the World Bank meet on a post-war prosperity plan, with a separate security-guarantees session on Thursday.
Source: byteseu.com.

item.title: Israel: Eisenkot now favourite for the mandate
item.description:
President Isaac Herzog's consultations moved decisively toward Gadi Eisenkot on Thursday.
United Torah Judaism — a Netanyahu ally in the previous five elections — declined to recommend any candidate, a major setback for the prime minister. The Arab-led Ra'am list endorsed Eisenkot, as did the Democrats, while Otzma Yehudit backed Netanyahu.
Herzog meets Likud and Eisenkot's Yashar party on Thursday evening to close the consultations, and has until November 11 to decide who gets the first 28 days to try to form a government. With 48 opposition seats plus 19 Arab-led recommendations, Eisenkot is now the favourite for the mandate — though a recommendation is not the same as a governing coalition, and he has ruled out governing with the Arab parties.
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Cyber: the TV-box botnet built by the manufacturer
item.description:
Google and partners dismantled XCPE, a botnet hidden in the firmware of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes across 200+ countries — a catch-up from Google Threat Intelligence Group's November 2 report.
Google says with high confidence that the manufacturer, Videostrong Technology Co., intentionally built and ran the backdoor for financial gain, renting the boxes out for ad fraud, proxy traffic and malware delivery. The backdoor ran with system privileges, loaded only after first boot so it dodged certification checks, and reinstalled itself if removed.
Google took legal action against the command-and-control domains, banned Videostrong from making certified Android devices, and says the takedown also severed access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
Source: plume.com.

item.title: Cyber: WordPress upgrade flaw now has a public exploit
item.description:
A working public proof of concept for WordPress CVE-2026-119977 was published on GitHub on November 4.
The flaw is a race condition in WordPress Core's update process (versions 4.7 through 7.1.3) that lets an unauthenticated attacker run PHP code on the server. CISA added it to the exploited-vulnerabilities catalog on November 3, and Wordfence blocked more than 12,000 attacks in a 24-hour window.
The federal remediation deadline is tomorrow, November 6 — update to WordPress 7.1.4. No new CISA KEV additions on November 5; the catalog stands at 1,768 entries.
Source: threatdefence.com.

item.title: Russian strikes force Ukraine's nuclear plants to cut output as Kyiv's water comes back — and Zelensky briefs US envoys ahead of Abu Dhabi
item.description:
Ukraine's Energy Ministry said on November 4 that Russian strikes forced the country's nuclear plants to reduce output, Crisis.Zone reports, without naming the plants or saying how far output fell. The ministry said the return to nominal levels will be gradual, "as soon as energy workers restore the networks damaged by the shelling." The Kyiv Post's explanation, carried in the same report, is that strikes on substations and transmission lines — not on reactors — are what force the plants to throttle back, a pattern Kyiv is now framing as a European nuclear-safety issue.
The details behind that cut are stark. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said Russia used 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles in the overnight attack of November 2–3, which grid operator Ukrenergo described as one of the most extensive on the energy system; energy facilities were hit more than 20 times in 24 hours. Three of DTEK's five thermal plants stopped generating, according to Reuters, and Shmyhal said Russia directed three drones at a substation critical to the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant — a step he said Ukraine reported to the IAEA. Russia's Defence Ministry, by contrast, claimed it hit four power plants and two substations, according to the Institute for the Study of War — a claim that describes the same campaign from the attacker's side and does not address the civilian outages. By Wednesday morning, Ukrenergo had cancelled emergency outages in Kyiv and most regions, returning them to scheduled hourly cuts, but Kharkiv region stayed on emergency cuts and some regions faced rationing of up to 16 hours a day.
For ordinary people, the human impact is in the taps and the heating as much as the lights. Most of Kyiv went more than 24 hours without running water after the November 3 strikes cut power to water facilities — the Kyiv Independent called it the most serious water outage in Kyiv since the war began — before the city water utility said on November 4 that all pumping stations were operating normally again and network pressure had stabilised. Warming centres were set up in the hardest-hit Kyiv districts, a day after the city began connecting residential buildings to heating. On the other side of the front, Russian-installed authorities in occupied Crimea said Ukrainian strikes caused widespread emergency outages on November 4, affecting Sevastopol, Simferopol and Kerch, with a Sevastopol schedule of two hours of power followed by six without — though officials also cited an external technical incident, and the primary cause could not be independently verified.
Diplomatically, Wednesday filled in the run-up to Abu Dhabi. President Volodymyr Zelensky had a "very detailed" discussion with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Independent's live blog reports, covering air defence — including Patriot interceptors — and Ukraine's proposals, which he said have been given to the American side. The European Commission's Wednesday session in Brussels, EuropeSays reports, was about refining scenarios for Ukraine's post-war economic development and prosperity, following up on earlier Miami talks, with a separate security-guarantee session due Thursday. Zelensky said another Brussels meeting takes place Thursday. ISW's assessment, carried by Crisis.Zone, reads the Russian campaign as aimed at "inflicting increasing costs on Ukrainian society and coercing Ukraine into capitulating over the winter" — which is exactly what the nuclear-output cut, the water outage and the 16-hour rationing look like from the ground.
In short: no reactor was hit, but the grid around them was hit hard enough to throttle nuclear output, Kyiv's water is back after its worst outage of the war, Kharkiv is still on emergency cuts — and with Brussels meeting again Thursday and Abu Dhabi set for November 10–11, Zelensky's message to the US envoys was air defence first.
Sources:
Source: crisis.zone.

item.title: Riyadh airport kept operating on Wednesday despite the Houthi missile claim — while Tehran reads the US midterms as a vote against war
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis claimed on Wednesday that a ballistic missile "directly" hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, causing what spokesman Yahya Saree called significant damage, Demócrata reports, alongside the other Wednesday operations already covered in the evening brief. The counter-evidence arrived the same evening: flight tracking reviewed by The Contrail shows the airport operating on Wednesday, with no delays flagged and about 15 departures cancelled — in line with recent days — and Saudi Arabia has not confirmed any damage. Saree again urged airlines and passengers to avoid Saudi airspace except over Mecca and Medina.
The two sides' positions are now easy to state plainly. The Houthis say the airport is a military target and unsafe, and have claimed repeated hits on it since October 7–11, when attacks killed at least 20 people by one tally. The airlines' behaviour tells a different story from either claim alone: most foreign carriers are still staying away — Etihad has now extended its Riyadh cancellations through November 19, Air France to December 12, Cathay Pacific to January 31, and British Airways' return is reportedly set for January 11 — while Saudi airlines keep flying, Saudia having moved most of its Riyadh flights to other Saudi airports through about December 1. Australia escalated its travel advice in the same window, Smartraveller warning travellers not to visit Saudi Arabia's airports in the current volatility, the Houthis having named Aramco targets as well.
For ordinary people, the practical point is that "open" and "normal" are not the same thing in Riyadh right now: the airport is operating, but largely on Saudi airlines, with most foreign routes still suspended into November, December or beyond — and every new claim, confirmed or not, gives airlines another reason to push their return dates back. In Tehran, meanwhile, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Wednesday that the US midterm results reflected growing public opposition to the war against Iran, AnewZ reports — a political reading of an American election, not a change in the battlefield, where Iran's position remains that the Strait of Hormuz reopens only if Washington meets its seven conditions, a position Rezaei repeated as "not convincing" on Tuesday. No new US–Iran deal was announced Wednesday.
In short: the Houthis claimed a direct hit on Riyadh airport, the airport kept operating and Riyadh has not confirmed damage, foreign airlines keep pushing their returns back — and Tehran is spinning the midterms while holding its Hormuz conditions unchanged.
Sources:
Source: thecontrail.org.

item.title: Tencent Hy4 — a 770-billion-parameter model that can see and use a computer, but the weights aren't out yet:
item.description:
Tencent switched on the full Hy4 on November 4: a 770B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (49B active per token, 1M-token context) that, unlike the text-only August preview, can interpret images, charts and documents and operate software through graphical interfaces and command lines.
The catch the headlines skip: on launch day Hy4 is hosted only — through Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy/CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, ima and APIs on OpenRouter and others — with weights and a system card promised "in the coming days." Until they land, nobody outside Tencent can download, run or fine-tune it, so treat "open-source" here as announced, not yet delivered.
Tencent's own computer-use benchmark puts Hy4 at 78.9 on OSWorld 2.1, behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 81.8 in Tencent's table — company-reported, not independently reproduced. Sources:
Source: startupfortune.com.

item.title: Komyshuvakha toll rises to 40 as Brussels talks on Ukraine's security guarantees open
item.description:
The death toll from Russia's bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, rose to 40 on Wednesday, Reuters reports, with dozens still missing as search-and-rescue work entered its third day. Regional official Ivan Fedorov put the missing at 59, while President Volodymyr Zelensky said more than 30 people may still be trapped under the rubble. Two rescue workers and four police officers are among the dead, according to Ukraine's emergency services. The Institute for the Study of War, in its November 4 assessment, likewise puts the toll at at least 40 and notes the strike hit a humanitarian aid station southeast of Zaporizhzhia city.
Zelensky's account, repeated in the Reuters reporting, is that Russian forces first dropped aerial bombs on an underground school building being used as a distribution point as people arrived to collect aid, then struck the shelter with more bombs — a "double-tap" pattern, as the Kyiv Independent's coverage, carried by EuropeSays, describes it, with nine guided aerial bombs reported. Reuters also reports verified bodycam footage from one of the policemen killed, showing residents rushing into an underground shelter moments before a large explosion. Russia's defence ministry, by contrast, maintains the attack targeted Ukrainian military units around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements, killing up to 25 servicemen — a claim that does not explain the reported civilian toll at an aid site and has not been independently verified. Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilians.
For ordinary people in the village, the practical consequences are immediate and grim: the regional administration said the Zaporizhzhia budget will cover funeral costs, with moderate-injury victims receiving about Hr.20,000 (about $440) and severe-injury victims up to about Hr.50,000 (about $1,100), according to EuropeSays. More broadly, the strike landed a day after a brief US-brokered local ceasefire for evacuations from occupied Oleshky expired, and less than a week before US envoy Steve Witkoff's Abu Dhabi talks on November 10–11, which are to cover post-war security agreements, de-escalation and humanitarian measures. On Wednesday, officials from Ukraine, the United States, Germany, France, Britain, NATO and the European Union met at the European Commission's headquarters in Brussels on security guarantees, reconstruction and post-war economic opportunities — the meeting already flagged in the morning brief, with a separate NATO security-guarantee session due Thursday. No outcome from Wednesday's Brussels session had been reported in the coverage checked by brief time.
In short: 40 dead in Komyshuvakha, 59 missing by one official count, more than 30 possibly still under rubble, Russia still claiming a military target — and in Brussels, the allies spent Wednesday trying to turn security-guarantee talk into something Kyiv can take to Abu Dhabi.
Sources:
Source: mymixfm.com.

item.title: Houthis claim a new round of Saudi strikes as Turkey's pact vote looms — and Riyadh stays silent on the airport claim
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis claimed a fresh series of strikes against Saudi targets on Wednesday, according to Demócrata's account of spokesman Yahya Saree's statements: a ballistic missile that "directly" hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, causing what Saree called significant damage, plus a drone strike on a radar installation on the Al Qahma peninsula, a ballistic missile on a camp in Najran, a strike on a Border Guard command-and-control building in Jizan, six ballistic missiles on Saudi reinforcements east of Al Jawf governorate, and a downed reconnaissance drone over Taiz. Saree again urged airlines, workers and passengers to avoid Saudi airspace, except over Mecca and Medina. Saudi authorities had not provided an official version of the airport claim by the time of that reporting — so the airport hit, like the morning's claim, remains unverified, and should be read as a Houthi claim, not a confirmed strike.
The backdrop has not eased. The US Mission in Saudi Arabia warned American citizens on Monday of potential Houthi attacks, airspace closures and flight disruptions, the Philippine News Agency reports, noting the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two drones over the Riyadh region on Monday, and that civil-defence alerts for Khamis Mushait, Abha, Taif and Najran were later lifted. A separate Dubai Standard roundup notes Hormuz traffic has collapsed — only five commodity-carrying ships passed through on Saturday, none on Sunday, against more than 130 a day before the conflict — and Brent crude was trading around $103 a barrel on Wednesday morning. Meanwhile Turkey's parliament was set on Wednesday to ratify the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, Reuters reported in the morning, with a collective-defence clause mirroring NATO's Article 5; ratification alone would not send Turkish troops, which need a separate mandate. No confirmed vote result had appeared in English-language coverage checked by 5 PM CT, so this brief does not claim the pact passed — watch the night brief for the result.
For ordinary people, the through-line is travel and fuel: Riyadh airport claims, confirmed or not, keep airlines and passengers guessing, US staff face tighter travel rules, and Gulf shipping remains a fraction of normal, which is exactly the pressure Iran and the Houthis are applying while Tehran says Washington's answer to its seven conditions is still "not convincing."
In short: the Houthis claimed a Wednesday missile hit on Riyadh airport plus five other operations, Riyadh has not confirmed the airport claim, US warnings to citizens stand, Hormuz traffic is near-empty — and Turkey's pact ratification was due Wednesday, with its result still unconfirmed at brief time.
Sources:
Source: democrata.es.

item.title: Poland — most Poles back neither side in the tribunal crisis, new polls say:
item.description:
A United Surveys/IBRiS poll for Wirtualna Polska, published Tuesday, found 38.6% of Poles believe neither Prime Minister Donald Tusk's government nor President Karol Nawrocki is right in the Constitutional Tribunal dispute, against 28.7% backing Nawrocki and 26.6% backing Tusk's government; among 18–29-year-olds, 64% sided with neither.
A separate Europion Polska poll for Onet (November 1–2) found 30% supporting the judges behind the tribunal leadership's suspension against 21% backing the existing leadership. Separately, the International Commission of Jurists criticised both the group of judges who suspended the tribunal's president and deputy and Nawrocki's refusal to swear in five parliament-elected judges.
No new Tusk–Nawrocki meeting date was announced Wednesday; the presidential palace has said a meeting could happen within days. Sources:
Source: hungarianconservative.com.

item.title: Apple — Siri AI opens to every developer in the iOS 27.3 beta, but users won't see it for months:
item.description:
Apple announced November 3 that a Developer Preview in the iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3 and visionOS 27.3 betas lets any developer bring an app's content and actions into Siri AI via App Intents, with new "skills" to chain several actions into one experience.
This is a testing surface, not a launch: App Store submissions with Siri AI integrations open in spring 2027, first customer integrations arrive "in a few months," and Siri AI remains unavailable in the EU on iOS, iPadOS and watchOS and for users under 13. Apple is running developer labs November 4–5.
Sources:
Source: eweek.com.
